lessons.title: Pages that seal: blocks and hashes
lessons.content:
# Pages that seal: blocks and hashes

A **blockchain** is a public book with a special filing rule. New pages, called **blocks**, include a fingerprint of the previous page. Rewriting an old transfer means rewriting every page after it, in public, against a network that will not agree with your private copy.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain a block without saying “crypto magic,” say what a **hash** is for, and tell a friend why a pretty screenshot is not the book.

## A ledger, again, with a filing rule

Crypto Foundations called a **ledger** the official list of balances and transfers. A bank ledger is private. Staff, software, and courts decide who may read it and who may change it. A blockchain ledger is copied by many computers, and the rule for adding a page is public.

That is the whole design bet in one sentence: **publish the book, and make quiet edits expensive.**

It is not a bet that prices are honest. It is not a bet that every token named Crystal Stones is the project. It is not a bet that you cannot lose a key. It is a filing rule.

A village savings group’s notebook is a ledger. If the secretary erases a line and nobody else has a copy, the group may never know. A blockchain is closer to this: every serious participant keeps a copy, and each new page is sealed so that yesterday’s pages are awkward to rewrite without everyone noticing.

## A block is a sealed page, not a coin

A **block** is a batch of recent transactions plus some filing data: a time, a reference to the previous block, and a hash. Think of a day’s worth of signed slips stapled together, then stamped, then the stamp copied onto the next day’s cover.

**Height** is how many pages from the start. Block 0 is the **genesis** block — the first page. You do not need the birthday. You need the picture: the book has an order.

People say “it is in a block” as if that were a blessing. Inclusion in a block means: this instruction was packed into a sealed page that the network is currently treating as official. It does not mean the token is a good investment. It does not mean the person who sent it is honest. It means the book accepted a signed instruction.

## A hash is a fingerprint, not encryption

A **hash function** takes any input — a page, a file, a sentence — and produces a short, fixed-length fingerprint. Change one comma, the fingerprint changes completely. For the functions these networks use, you cannot usefully work backwards from the fingerprint to the original.

Block N contains the hash of block N−1. If you tamper with an old transfer, block N−1’s hash changes, so block N no longer points at it, so block N+1 breaks too. Everyone else’s copy still has the old chain. Your rewrite is fanfic.

This is why people say a blockchain is “immutable.” That word is too loud. A more precise beginner sentence: **this book’s history is expensive to quietly rewrite, because each page is glued to the previous fingerprint.**

It is not encryption. Encryption hides. A hash does not hide the page. The page is public. The hash only proves “this is the page we fingerprinted,” the way a wax seal proves a letter was not swapped after it left the office.

TABLE
Word | Plain meaning | What beginners get wrong
Block | A sealed page of recent transactions plus a fingerprint of the previous page | “A block is a coin”
Hash | A fingerprint of data; change the data, change the print | “A hash is a password”
Height | How many pages from the start | “Higher height means a better investment”
Chain | Pages linked by fingerprints | “All chains are one book with nicknames”
Genesis | The first page | “I need to read it to use a wallet”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Chidi’s cousin sends a link to a “private blockchain explorer.” The page is beautiful. It shows 4,000 USDT arriving in Chidi’s address, with a hash, a block number, and a green tick.

1. Chidi opens the real public explorer for the chain he actually uses — for this academy, BscScan for BNB Smart Chain — from a bookmark, not from the cousin’s link.
2. He pastes his address. There is no such transfer.
3. He pastes the hash from the pretty page. The real explorer does not know it.
4. He does not ship goods. He does not send “verification BNB.” He closes the tab.
5. The cousin hashed a pretty HTML page. They did not add a page to the book the network actually runs. Fingerprints on a fake site are decoration.

DIAGRAM
Block 100  --> hash-of-100 sits inside Block 101
Block 101  --> hash-of-101 sits inside Block 102
Block 102  --> hash-of-102 sits inside Block 103
        |
        v
Change one transfer in 100
        |
        v
hash-of-100 changes --> 101 no longer points at it --> 102 and 103 break
        |
        v
Honest nodes still have the old chain. Your rewrite is ignored.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this does not mean

Say these so they stick, because this is where slogans start:

- It does not mean the **price** of a token is honest.
- It does not mean a token named Crystal Stones on a clone contract is the project.
- It does not mean you cannot lose keys. The book can be public and your secret can still walk.
- It does not mean every chain is equally hard to lean on. Who writes the next page is the next lesson.
- It does not mean a screenshot of a hash is a payment.

It means **this book’s history is expensive to quietly rewrite.** That is a filing fact. Treat it as a filing fact.

## How wallets and explorers use this without you seeing it

Your phone wallet does not usually store the entire book. It asks a helper computer for “what does this address hold?” and “please broadcast this signed page-request.” An explorer like **BscScan** is a searchable window onto the same book. Both are views. The book is the network’s copies of sealed pages.

If the view lies, the book may still be honest. That is why this course will make you open the explorer yourself, from a bookmark, until it is boring. You do not need to compute a hash by hand. You need to know why BscScan’s history for a transaction is a better argument than a WhatsApp screenshot with a green tick drawn on it.

NOTE
Academy rule: you do not need to compute a hash by hand, and this classroom will not pretend you do. You need to know why a public explorer’s history for a transaction is a better argument than a screenshot. If someone will not give you a hash you can paste into the real explorer, they have not shown you a page of the book.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are here so that “blockchain” stops being a mood and becomes a filing system: sealed pages, fingerprints, a public copy, an expensive rewrite. Module 2 will name one specific book — BNB Smart Chain, chain ID 56. Module 5 will make you read that book until the tabs are ordinary. None of that is a buy order.

## Say this out loud

- A blockchain is a public ledger whose new pages include a fingerprint of the previous page.
- A block is a sealed page of transactions, not a coin and not a blessing.
- A hash is a fingerprint. Change the page, change the print. It is not a password and not encryption.
- Quiet rewrites fail because honest copies still have the old fingerprints.
- A fake explorer can hash a pretty page. That is decoration, not the book.

Next: who is allowed to write the next page — miners versus validators, in beginner language.

lessons.title: Who writes the next page (miners vs validators)
lessons.content:
# Who writes the next page (miners vs validators)

If anyone can add any page, the book is graffiti. If only one office can add a page, you have a company database with extra branding. Public chains sit in between: many participants compete or take turns under a published rule.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say, in plain words, what a **miner** does, what a **validator** does, why BNB Smart Chain is not Bitcoin, and why your phone wallet is usually a guest at someone else’s computer.

## If anyone can write, the book is graffiti

A public ledger still needs a **writer rule**. Without one, two people could publish two different “next pages,” each claiming to spend the same coins, and the copies would split forever. That is the **double-spend problem** from Foundations, now as a staffing question: **who is allowed to propose the next sealed page?**

The network answers with a **consensus** rule. Consensus here is not a group chat about whether you are a good person. It is a rule for one question: **which page is the next official page?**

Your job as a beginner is not to become a researcher. Your job is to notice that “it is on the blockchain” is an incomplete sentence. Which book? Who writes pages on that book? How expensive is a cheat?

## Proof of Work, in beginner language

**Proof of Work (PoW)** is Bitcoin’s original style. Machines burn electricity racing to find a rare hash. The winner proposes a block. Other machines check that the page follows the rules, then they start racing for the next one.

Why burn energy? To make a long fake history expensive. To rewrite a week of Bitcoin pages you would need to outrun the honest energy of the network for that week, in public. That cost is the point. It is also why Bitcoin is slower and why fees can be high when many people want space on the next page.

A **miner** is a participant who spends that energy to propose pages. A **mining pool** is a group of miners sharing work and rewards. Pools can concentrate power. “Many machines” is not the same as “many independent decision-makers.” Hold both facts.

## Proof of Stake, and the BSC flavour

**Proof of Stake (PoS)** is a different cost model. **Validators** lock coins (**stake**) and risk them if they cheat. Instead of burning electricity to race, they take turns or get chosen under a published rule. Cheating is supposed to cost the staked coins.

BNB Smart Chain uses a **Proof of Staked Authority** style design: a limited, named set of validators produce blocks. It is faster and cheaper than Bitcoin. It is also a **different trust story**. You are trusting a smaller writer set more than you trust “anyone with a mining warehouse.”

This academy will not pretend those two sentences are a PhD. You need the beginner consequence:

TABLE
Design | Who writes the next page | Beginner consequence
Bitcoin Proof of Work | Miners racing with energy | Slow, often expensive, extremely hard to quietly rewrite; not where Crystal Stones lives
Ethereum-style Proof of Stake | Validators who stake coins | A public chain with a different cost for cheating
BNB Smart Chain (staked authority flavour) | A limited validator set | Fast, cheap gas in BNB; a more concentrated writer set; EVM-like tools
A random new chain with a shiny logo | Unknown | Do not move rent money there because a logo is shiny
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A friend says “BSC is not a real blockchain because it has few validators.”

1. You do not defend a brand. You name objects.
2. You say: BSC **is** a blockchain — blocks, hashes, a public ledger, a writer rule.
3. You say: it has a **more concentrated** writer set than Bitcoin. That concentration is why fees are low and why some people prefer Bitcoin or Ethereum for large settlement.
4. You say: Crystal Stones lives on BSC as a BEP-20 token. That is geography, not a holiness ranking.
5. You use BSC for practice **knowing that tradeoff**, not pretending it is Bitcoin, and not pretending it is “fake” because it is not Bitcoin.

DIAGRAM
Users broadcast signed transactions
        |
        v
Miners (PoW) or validators (PoS / BSC) pack a block
        |
        v
Other nodes check the rules and append the page
        |
        v
Explorers and wallets read the result
        |
        v
Your phone is usually in this last box — a reader, not the whole book
ENDDIAGRAM

## A node is a copy of the book; your phone usually is not

A **node** is a computer running the software that stores and checks the book. A **full node** keeps enough history to check the rules itself. An **RPC** is a counter on a node: a way for wallets and apps to ask questions (“what does this address hold?”) and to submit signed transactions.

Your phone wallet is usually **not** a full node. It asks an RPC. That is why a malicious RPC or a fake app can lie even when the chain is honest. The book can be public and your window can still be a lie.

Running your own node is a later skill. Today: know that you are usually a guest at someone else’s RPC, and that BscScan is a widely used window, not a pope.

## The tradeoff you actually live with

Bitcoin’s cost is energy and slowness. Ethereum’s cost is gas that can spike. BSC’s cost is a smaller validator set. **There is no free rail.**

This academy teaches BSC because Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 on that book, because USDT-on-BSC is a practical rail for later paid-track checkout, and because cheap, fast blocks are how beginners survive their first practice sends. We will not pretend that choice is ideologically pure. We will teach you to name it.

When someone says “BSC = Bitcoin,” they have smashed two books into one word. Bitcoin is a chain with a PoW writer rule and a native coin called bitcoin. BNB Smart Chain is a different book, chain ID 56, native coin BNB, validator-style writers. Same idea of sealed pages. Not the same staff, not the same coin, not the same fees.

NOTE
Academy rule: “more concentrated than Bitcoin” is a precise sentence, not an insult and not a reason to send a seed to a stranger who promises a “decentralised upgrade.” Running your own node is optional. Knowing that you are usually asking someone else’s RPC is not optional.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a staffing model for a public book: miners race, validators take turns or get chosen, BSC uses a small named set on purpose. The next lesson is why the industry shipped many books instead of one, and why that fact will try to empty a beginner’s wallet.

## Say this out loud

- Someone has to write the next page under public rules, or the book is graffiti or a private office.
- Proof of Work makes cheating expensive with energy. Proof of Stake makes cheating expensive with staked coins. They are different cost models, not different religions.
- BNB Smart Chain is a real blockchain with a smaller validator set than Bitcoin — a tradeoff, not a spell, and not “Bitcoin with a yellow logo.”
- A node stores and checks the book. A phone wallet usually asks an RPC instead of being the whole book.
- A malicious RPC can lie about balances even when the chain is honest.

Next: why there is not one chain to rule them all.

lessons.title: Why many chains exist
lessons.content:
# Why many chains exist

Beginners want one chain, one coin, one app. The industry shipped dozens. That is not only greed — though greed is present. It is also different design choices: different writer rules, different fee markets, different programming engines, different communities.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say that many chains means many books, not many nicknames for one book, and you should be able to refuse a bridge because a group dropped a URL.

## Different jobs, not different stickers

A **chain** is a ledger with its own pages, its own native coin, its own writer set, and its own rules. Tokens on that chain are rows in contracts on that book. They do not automatically exist on another book.

Rough beginner map, without worship:

- **Bitcoin**: conservative settlement, Proof of Work, native bitcoin. Slow on purpose.
- **Ethereum**: a world computer for **smart contracts** — programs stored on the chain — often more expensive when busy.
- **BNB Smart Chain**: Ethereum-like contracts, cheaper fees, different validator story, huge retail activity. This course’s home book.
- **Others** (Solana, Tron, and a long list): other speed, fee, and tooling bets.

None of these is “the official chain of crypto.” Crypto is not a company. It is a family of public-ledger designs. People who say “just use the blockchain” without naming which one are either selling or lost.

## EVM compatibility is a shape, not a shared balance

**EVM** means **Ethereum Virtual Machine** — the engine that runs contracts on Ethereum. BSC is **EVM-compatible**. That is why:

- addresses look like Ethereum (0x and forty hex characters)
- a wallet app such as MetaMask — an **example of a wallet app**, not an endorsement — can add BSC as a network
- a contract written for Ethereum can often be deployed on BSC

It is also why people send funds to the “same address” on the wrong network. Compatibility of **shape** is not a shared **balance**. The letters can match. The books do not merge.

This is the sentence you will reuse until it is a reflex: **same 0x text, different planet.**

## Bridges sit between books, and they are how people lose funds

A token on one book does not automatically exist on another. **Bridges** try to represent value across books, usually by locking on one side and minting a representation on the other. That extra machine is extra trust. Bridges are a major hack magnet.

This Basic course’s rule is blunt: **do not bridge practice funds because a group dropped a URL.** Module 4 will give bridges one honest lesson of their own. Today you only need the geography: bridges are not a dropdown that “makes the chains one chain.” They are a separate, risky system.

TABLE
You see | True meaning | Beginner move
Same 0x address on Ethereum and BSC | Same key can speak both books; balances are separate | Watch the network chip, then the explorer of that network
“We bridged it” | A different, risky system now holds a claim | Do not follow a chat-group bridge
“It’s the same MetaMask” | The app can switch books; it does not merge them | Switching the dropdown does not move coins
“USDT is USDT” | Ticker stickers collide; ERC-20 USDT and BEP-20 USDT are different objects | Name the chain, then the contract
A clone “Crystal Stones” on another chain | A different contract, usually a trap | Verify the BSC contract; do not chase the name
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 on BNB Smart Chain. A clone deploys “Crystal Stones” on Ethereum or on a random extra chain. The name matches. The logo matches. A caption says “we are now multi-chain, bridge here to get the real one.”

1. Sam opens the project’s long-standing site — not a Google ad, not a pinned tweet from an account created yesterday.
2. She copies the published contract: 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
3. She pastes it into BscScan, on the real domain. That is the object this academy means.
4. She does not bridge into the clone. She does not add the clone by name search.
5. BscScan still shows the real contract on chain 56. The clone is a different object. The name was a sticker.

DIAGRAM
Bitcoin book          Ethereum book         BNB Smart Chain book        Tron book
   |                       |                        |                      |
 native BTC           ETH + ERC-20              BNB + BEP-20           TRX + TRC-20
   |                       |                        |                      |
   +------- bridges sit BETWEEN books. Extra trust. Extra hacks. ---------+

Crystal Stones, as this academy references it, lives on the BSC book.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Crystal Stones lives on one book unless the project itself publishes otherwise

This academy’s default practice network is BNB Smart Chain. Crystal Stones, as the project publishes it, is a BEP-20 there. If the project ever truly lived elsewhere, that would be a slow public fact you could verify on more than a Friday-night DM. Treat surprise “we migrated, bridge now” messages as clones.

Academy tuition rails, when you reach paid tracks, are USDT on **BNB Smart Chain**, not “USDT somewhere.” The multiplicity of chains is why that sentence is so picky. USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout is not Crystal Stones token and not some other brand. Geography first.

## How to talk about “the chain” without lying

Useful beginner sentences:

- “I am on BNB Smart Chain, chain ID 56.”
- “I need BNB for gas on that book.”
- “This USDT is the BEP-20 one, not the Ethereum one.”
- “This token’s identity is the contract address, not the name.”

Useless beginner sentences:

- “It’s on the blockchain.”
- “USDT is USDT.”
- “Same address so it will arrive.”
- “BSC is Bitcoin.”

NOTE
Academy rule: we teach BSC because Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 and because USDT-on-BSC is a practical rail. That is curriculum geography, not a commandment to ignore Bitcoin forever, and not a commandment to bridge because a caption said “multi-chain.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a map of many books. Compatibility of tools is not a merged balance. Bridges are optional and, for this track, later and dangerous. The next lesson is what happens after you press send: pending, included, buried — and why “I sent it” is not cash.

## Say this out loud

- Many chains means many books, not many nicknames for one book.
- EVM-compatible means similar tools and address shape, not shared balances.
- Same 0x letters on Ethereum and BSC are not the same pile of coins.
- Bridges sit between books. They are extra trust. Basic does not use them because a group dropped a URL.
- Crystal Stones lives on BNB Smart Chain unless you can verify otherwise from more than a chat message — and verifying is not a buy order.

Next: confirmations, finality, and why “0/1” is not a payment.

lessons.title: Confirmations and finality for a beginner
lessons.content:
# Confirmations and finality for a beginner

A transaction is **broadcast**, then **included in a block**, then **buried under more blocks**. Those stages are not the same. A wallet banner that says “submitted” is not a payment. A shopkeeper who ships against a screenshot is making a donation.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to wait like an adult: pending is not paid, one confirmation is young, burial is stronger, and you will not import Bitcoin’s folklore blindly onto BNB Smart Chain.

## Broadcast: you spoke; the book has not sealed a page

Your wallet sent a signed message to an RPC. The **mempool** is the waiting room of instructions not yet packed into a block. Explorers may show **pending**. Pending is not paid. It can vanish, be replaced, or sit until the gas price is acceptable to whoever is writing pages.

“I sent it” in a chat is a human sentence. It is not a ledger sentence. The ledger sentence is: **is this hash included in a block on the book we agreed to watch?**

If the RPC never accepted it, or the fee is too low, or the nonce is stuck (Module 4), the book does not have a page yet. Refreshing the app does not create a page. Shouting in a WhatsApp group does not create a page.

## Included: one confirmation is real and young

When a validator packs the transaction into a block, you have **one confirmation**. This is real-but-young. On busy chains, rare **reorganisations** — the network switching a very recent page for another valid page — can still shuffle the youngest blocks.

For a shop selling a small item, 1 confirmation on BSC is often treated as “probably fine.” For a large over-the-counter receive, people wait longer. For a stranger demanding shipment of a phone against a “submitted” banner, you wait until the explorer shows success, the right token contract, the right amount, your address.

**Finality**, in conversation, means: reversing this would be hard enough that we will treat it as settled. Different chains have different gadgets and different speeds. Do not import Bitcoin’s “wait 6 blocks” folklore blindly onto BSC, and do not treat 0 confirmations as cash.

## Buried: each new page on top is another confirmation

Each new block on top of yours is another **confirmation**. Burial is stronger than inclusion. On a fast chain, burial happens quickly. That is a feature for retail. It is not a reason to skip the pending stage.

BSC is fast. Bitcoin is slow. Ethereum has its own finality gadgets. The skill is: **name the stage, then name the chain, then decide whether this receive is large enough to wait.**

TABLE
Stage | What happened | Shopkeeper meaning
Broadcast / pending | Signed message is in a waiting room, or sitting at an RPC | Not paid
1 confirmation on BSC | Packed into a block | Usually accepted for small goods; still wait for your own large receives
Many confirmations | More pages on top | The argument gets easier
Replaced / dropped | A different transaction took that nonce, or the fee was ignored | You are not paid; check nonce and gas later in this course
Success on explorer, wrong token | A transfer happened, but not the contract you care about | You were not paid in the asset you named
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A buyer sends Crystal Stones and immediately demands shipment based on a wallet “submitted” banner.

1. Amaka does not ship. She asks for the transaction hash.
2. She opens BscScan from a bookmark. She pastes the hash.
3. The explorer still says pending. She still does not ship.
4. A few minutes later the first hash disappears. The buyer raised gas on a **different** transaction and the first one died. A new hash appears, or none does.
5. If she had shipped at “submitted,” she would have shipped for free. She waits until the explorer shows success, the Crystal Stones contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00, the right amount, her address.

DIAGRAM
Sign
  --> broadcast (pending)     not paid
        --> included in a block    young
              --> more blocks on top    safer to treat as paid
If it never leaves pending, you are not paid.
If a different nonce replacement lands instead, you are not paid for the first hash.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Do not mix folklore across books

Bitcoin culture says “wait six confirmations” for large receives. That number is a convention for that book, not a law of physics. BSC blocks are faster, so “six” is a different amount of wall-clock time and a different security story, because the writer set is different.

Two mistakes, both expensive:

- Treating BSC’s 0 confirmations as cash because “BSC is fast.”
- Waiting an hour for six Bitcoin-style confirmations on a 2-dollar test send and then calling the network broken.

Match the wait to the size and to the chain. For this academy’s practice amounts, “explorer says success, right token, right address” is the ritual. For amounts you would miss, wait longer, and still use the explorer, not the app banner.

## The shopkeeper rule, written once so you can reuse it

Never take “I sent it” as final. Take the explorer status for the hash. Confirm:

- status success, not pending, not failed
- the token contract you named, not a lookalike
- the amount
- your address as the recipient of that token transfer

This is the same muscle as the exchanges course, now with vocabulary. Module 5 will make each explorer tab boring. Today you only need the stages: broadcast, include, bury.

NOTE
Academy rule: shipment against a screenshot is a donation. Pending is not paid. A replaced transaction is not paid. Practice this on tiny amounts so the first time you care, the ritual is already in your hands.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have stages instead of a vibe. The next lesson opens the envelope: what fields actually sit inside a transaction, and why a USDT send can show 0 BNB value and still be real.

## Say this out loud

- Pending is broadcast, not paid. A “submitted” banner is not cash.
- Inclusion in a block is real and young. Burial under more blocks is stronger.
- Fast chains still have a pending stage. Do not skip it because BSC is cheap.
- Do not import Bitcoin’s “wait 6” as a superstition, and do not treat 0 confirmations as a payment.
- Shipment against a screenshot, or against the wrong token contract, is a donation.

Next: what is actually inside a transaction.

lessons.title: What a transaction contains
lessons.content:
# What a transaction contains

A **transaction** is a signed instruction. On EVM chains — Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, and cousins — it is not a photograph of money flying. It is a message that says: the holder of this key authorises this exact change, and here is the fuel money for the writer set.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name the fields that matter to a beginner, and you should know why sending a token often shows **value = 0** on the explorer’s native line.

## A signed instruction, not a screenshot

The important fields, in beginner language:

- **from** — the address whose key signed. This is the authority. If this key did not sign, this transaction is not from that person, no matter what a chat says.
- **to** — an address. It might be a person’s wallet (**externally owned account**), or it might be a **contract** — a program on the chain.
- **value** — native coin attached. On BSC that coin is **BNB**. On Ethereum it is ETH. Token sends often have value = 0 because the token movement lives inside the contract call.
- **data** — extra payload. Token transfers live here. So do approvals. So do drains. You do not need to read hex. You need to know this field exists.
- **gas limit / gas price** — how much fuel you allow, and what you bid per unit of work.
- **nonce** — a counter per sender, so your transactions have an order. Module 4 will make this painful and then useful.
- **signature** — proof the from-key approved this exact message. Change any field, the signature no longer matches.

A screenshot of a wallet can fake every one of these visually. The book cannot fake the signature without the key. That is why we paste hashes into explorers.

## Native send versus token send — the confusion that never dies

Sending **BNB** to a friend: **to** is the friend, **value** is the BNB, **data** is empty (or nearly empty). The explorer’s native value line is the story.

Sending **USDT** as a BEP-20 token: **to** is usually the **USDT contract**, **value** is usually 0, **data** says “transfer this amount to my friend.” The friend appears in the **token transfer** records, not only as **to**.

This is why people look at the wrong BscScan panel and panic. They see “BNB transferred: 0” and think the USDT failed. The token tab tells a different story.

Crystal Stones, as a BEP-20, behaves like that token send. You are not mailing a rock. You are asking the Crystal Stones contract to update its list: subtract from you, add to them. The contract address is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Verifying that address is not a buy order.

## Approvals and swaps are transactions too

An **approval** is a transaction that tells a token contract: this **spender** may move up to N of my tokens later. Value is usually 0. It still costs gas in BNB. It is not “just connecting.” Module 4 will separate connect, sign, and approve. Today: know that an approval is a real on-chain instruction you can later see.

A **swap** on a decentralised exchange is usually a call to a **router** contract. **to** is the router. Value might be BNB if you are selling BNB. The token hops show up as several internal movements. One signature authorised the bundle. Module 5 will teach you not to panic at hops.

TABLE
Intent | to | value (native BNB) | Where the movement shows
Send BNB | Friend’s address | BNB amount | Transaction value
Send USDT (BEP-20) | USDT contract | Usually 0 | Token transfer records
Send Crystal Stones | Crystal Stones contract | Usually 0 | Token transfer records
Approve a spender | Token contract | 0 | Approval / event; spender may pull later
Swap on a DEX | Router contract | Maybe BNB | Several internal hops plus token transfers
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student sends 20 USDT on BSC to pay a freelancer.

1. They copy the freelancer’s 0x from a channel they already trust, after confirming the network chip is BSC.
2. They send. BscScan overview shows “BNB transferred: 0.”
3. They think it failed. They almost send again.
4. They open **Token transferred**. It shows 20 USDT, from them, to the freelancer, status success.
5. They do not send again. Native value and token value are different rows. Sending twice would have been a second payment.

DIAGRAM
Simple BNB send:
  you ---- value = BNB ----> friend

Token send (USDT, Crystal Stones, any BEP-20):
  you ---- value = 0, data = transfer ----> token contract
                                              |
                                              v
                                        friend’s token balance
                                        on that contract updates
ENDDIAGRAM

## You do not need to decode hex; you need the right tab

Input data on BscScan looks like a curse. You are not required to read it. You are required to:

- open the hash on the real explorer
- read status
- read **to** (person or contract?)
- read native value
- read token transfers (which contract, which amount, which recipient)
- read the fee in BNB

If those lines match the job, the transaction did the job. If a stranger wants you to paste input data into a “decoder” that then asks to connect a wallet, that is not homework. That is a trap.

NOTE
Academy rule: a transaction is a signed instruction, not a screenshot and not a chat claim. Token sends often show 0 BNB value. Look at token transfers. Approvals are transactions too. You will not be asked to decode hex in Basic, and you will not be asked to launch a token. Those are later, or never, depending on the track.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now open a hash and name the envelope. Module 1’s book metaphor is complete enough to use: pages, writers, many books, stages of settlement, fields inside an instruction. Module 2 names BNB Smart Chain as a specific book — chain ID 56, BNB for gas, BEP-20 tokens, the 0x trap.

## Say this out loud

- A transaction is a signed instruction. The key that signed **from** is the authority.
- Native **value** is BNB on this chain. Token sends often show 0 there because the movement is inside the contract call.
- When you send a BEP-20, **to** is usually the token contract, and the friend appears in token-transfer records.
- Approvals and swaps are transactions too. They still cost BNB gas.
- You do not need hex. You need the right BscScan tab, the right contract, the right amount, the right address.

Take the quiz. Module 2 names BNB Smart Chain as a specific book.

lessons.title: Why BSC exists in the first place
lessons.content:
# Why BSC exists in the first place

**BNB Smart Chain (BSC)** is an EVM-compatible public chain associated with Binance’s history. People use it because fees are usually low enough for small transfers, because wallet apps already know how to speak EVM, because a huge number of tokens — including Crystal Stones — live there as **BEP-20**, and because retail in Africa and Asia already met it through exchange withdrawals labelled BEP-20.

It is not “the official chain of crypto.” It is a popular book with a specific owner-history and a specific fee market. This lesson is history without worship.

By the end you should be able to separate three objects that share a yellow family resemblance: **Binance the company**, **BNB the coin**, and **BSC the chain**.

## Not the official chain of anything

Crypto is not a company with a headquarters that picks a winner. Bitcoin does not appoint BSC. Ethereum does not appoint BSC. Binance — **an example of a centralised exchange**, not “the only real one” — launched and promoted an EVM chain so that Ethereum-style apps could run with cheaper fees and with BNB as gas.

That is a product decision. Product decisions can be useful. They are not commandments. You can use BSC without loving the company. You can dislike the company and still need to read chain ID 56 because that is where a token you are verifying lives.

This academy teaches this book because Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 here, and because later paid-track checkout uses USDT on BEP-20. Curriculum geography. Not a personality test.

## EVM cousin: cheaper, faster, different trust

Ethereum showed that a public chain could run programs, not only simple payments. Those programs are **smart contracts**. When Ethereum is busy, **gas** — the fee for work — can spike. Small transfers feel silly. Retail looks for a cousin: same 0x shape, same wallet apps, lower fees.

BSC is that cousin. Faster blocks. Cheaper gas, usually paid in BNB. A smaller validator set, as Module 1 already named. You import Ethereum’s **tools** and also Ethereum’s **footguns**: unlimited approvals, fake tokens, phishing apps that look like dashboards.

“Cheaper and faster” is not “safer.” It is a different point on the slider. Adults pick rails on purpose.

## BNB the coin versus BSC the chain versus Binance the company

**BNB** started as an exchange token. It is also the **native coin** of BNB Smart Chain: it pays gas, and it can be sent as value. Holding BNB as an IOU on an exchange is not the same as holding BNB on-chain in a wallet you control. Same name, again. The wallets course already taught IOU versus on-chain. Keep it.

**BSC** is the book. Mainnet chain ID **56**. Explorer people actually use: **BscScan**. Native coin: BNB. Token standard: BEP-20.

**Binance the company** is a business. It can list tokens, freeze accounts, change withdrawal screens, and get regulated. Using BSC does not mean you have a Binance account. Having a Binance account does not mean you are already on-chain.

TABLE
Name | Role | Common smash-together
BNB | Native coin of BSC; pays gas; also a trading asset on venues | “I bought BNB on an exchange so I am on BSC”
BSC | The chain / book (chain ID 56 on mainnet) | “BSC is Binance, so it is not a blockchain”
BEP-20 | The token standard on that book, ERC-20-style | “BEP-20 is a kind of Bitcoin”
BscScan | A popular explorer for that book | “The explorer is the chain”
Binance | An example of a centralised exchange | “The company, the coin, and the chain are one object”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student buys “BNB” on an exchange and thinks they are already on BSC, ready to add Crystal Stones as a custom token.

1. They still have an IOU. The exchange’s ledger says the company owes them BNB.
2. They open a self-custody wallet — Trust Wallet or MetaMask as **examples of wallet apps**, not endorsements — and the BNB balance is 0 because nothing has been withdrawn.
3. They try to send a token. The wallet refuses: no gas.
4. They withdraw **BNB on the BSC network** (not Ethereum, not a leftover Beacon label, not a random “BNB Chain” fossil without reading the info icon) to their 0x.
5. After the explorer shows success, they have native gas in the wallet they will use. Buying the ticker on a venue was step zero, not arrival.

DIAGRAM
Binance the company  !=  BNB the coin  !=  BSC the chain

You can use BSC without loving the company.
You still need BNB on that chain to pay gas.
An exchange balance called BNB is an IOU until you withdraw it onto the book.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What “smart chain” is trying to say

**Smart contracts** are programs stored on the chain. Tokens, decentralised exchanges, and NFT markets are contracts. BSC copied Ethereum’s programming model so developers could deploy cheaply.

This course will **not** teach you Solidity. This course will **not** teach you how to launch a token. That is Advanced, and even there it is not a side hustle we will sell you. Today you only need: the book can hold programs, and those programs can keep lists of who holds a ticker.

That design imported Ethereum’s accidents. Fake BEP-20s are cheap to deploy. Approvals can drain you later. A “dashboard” can ask you to sign a permit. Safety is the next course. This course gives you the geography so Safety has nouns.

## Why this academy stays on this book for Basic

We could teach Bitcoin first as settlement religion. We did not, because your next practical tasks — verifying Crystal Stones, practising a BEP-20 receive, later paying tuition in USDT on BEP-20 — happen here. We could pretend all chains are equal. They are not. We name the tradeoff and we stay.

NOTE
This academy can teach BSC because Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 and because USDT-on-BSC is a practical rail. That is curriculum geography, not a commandment to ignore Bitcoin forever, and not a buy order for BNB, USDT, or Crystal Stones.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now say why BSC exists without worship and without sneering. Three objects, one book, BNB as gas. Next: the numbers wallets hide — chain ID, RPC, mainnet versus the practice book called testnet.

## Say this out loud

- BNB Smart Chain is an EVM-compatible public book with cheap-ish fees and a smaller validator set — a cousin of Ethereum, not Bitcoin, and not “the official chain.”
- BNB pays gas on that book. An exchange IOU named BNB is not yet gas in your wallet.
- BEP-20 is the token rule-set on that book.
- Company, coin, and chain are three objects. Smash them and you will withdraw to the wrong place.
- This classroom uses BSC as geography. It will not tell you to buy.

Next: the numbers wallets hide — chain ID 56, RPC, mainnet versus testnet.

lessons.title: Chain ID 56, RPC, mainnet vs testnet
lessons.content:
# Chain ID 56, RPC, mainnet vs testnet

Wallets pick a network from a dropdown. Under the dropdown are numbers. The numbers are the lesson. The dropdown is a sticker.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say **BNB Smart Chain mainnet is chain ID 56**, say what an **RPC** is without calling it a password, and treat **testnet** coins as fake — not local currency, not a salary, not a thing you sell in a P2P chat.

## Chain ID exists so a signature cannot be replayed on the wrong book

EVM chains have a **chain ID** so a signature meant for one book cannot be **replayed** on another. Replay would mean: you signed “pay 1 native coin to Sam” on one chain, and a thief broadcasts the same signature on a different chain where you also have funds.

- BNB Smart Chain **mainnet**: chain ID **56**
- BSC **testnet** (practice fake coins): a different ID (historically 97; if a UI shows something else, you are not on 56)
- Ethereum mainnet: chain ID 1

If a “support agent” sends an RPC and a chain ID that is not 56, you may be looking at a fork, a testnet, or a trap. Your real USDT will not be there. Your real Crystal Stones will not be there. The letters of your 0x might still look right. The book is wrong.

## RPC is a counter, not a church, and not a seed

The **RPC** is how a wallet talks to a node. It is a URL. Your wallet asks it questions and hands it signed transactions to broadcast. Official and well-known public RPCs exist. Wallet apps often bundle one.

Random RPCs in a Discord or WhatsApp can:

- lie about balances
- spy on your IP and addresses
- in nasty setups, try to get you to sign the wrong thing (the signing still happens in the wallet — stay awake)

An RPC is **not** a password. It is **not** your seed. If someone says “paste your seed into the RPC to connect faster,” they are stealing. If someone says “the RPC password is the twelve words,” they are stealing with extra vocabulary.

Adding a network by hand in MetaMask (example of a wallet app): name, RPC, chain ID **56**, symbol BNB, explorer https://bscscan.com. Prefer the wallet’s built-in BSC where it exists. Prefer a documented public RPC over a QR from a stranger.

## Mainnet is the book with real value; testnet is a practice book

**Mainnet** is the book with real value. Real BNB. Real BEP-20 USDT. Real Crystal Stones, if you ever hold them — this course does not require that.

**Testnet** is a playground with fake coins from a **faucet**. A faucet is a tap that gives practice units so developers and students can try transactions without lighting real money. Testnet Crystal Stones is not Crystal Stones. Testnet BNB is not BNB. Testnet coins are not worth local currency. Anyone offering to “buy your testnet BNB for cash” is either confused or running a social engineering drill.

Never send mainnet USDT to a testnet address because someone said “it is cheaper.” Different books. Different IDs. Fake money on one side, real money on the other.

TABLE
Network | Chain ID (BSC family) | Value | Beginner use
BSC mainnet | 56 | Real | This course’s book
BSC testnet | not 56 (historically 97) | Fake / practice | Optional playground; not a salary
Ethereum mainnet | 1 | Real, different book | Do not mix with BSC receives
A random “BSC Ultra” | whatever they typed | Assume hostile | Stop
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** MetaMask is on Ethereum mainnet (chain ID 1). A student pastes a BSC USDT receive address into a dApp that builds an Ethereum USDT transaction.

1. The 0x letters match their wallet. They feel safe.
2. They do not read the network chip. They sign.
3. USDT leaves on Ethereum. Their BSC wallet still shows the old BEP-20 balance, or shows nothing of this send.
4. The freelancer on BSC is not paid. A different book moved.
5. Correct ritual, every time: read the network chip **before** signing. For this academy, the chip should mean BSC, chain ID 56, when the job is BSC.

DIAGRAM
Wallet network chip
    |
    +--> BSC 56 + known RPC + bscscan.com  --> the book this course means
    +--> Ethereum 1                         --> different book, real money, not BSC
    +--> testnet (not 56)                   --> fake coins, not local currency
    +--> unknown chain ID + unknown RPC     --> stop
ENDDIAGRAM

## Bookmark the explorer yourself

Bookmark **bscscan.com** yourself. Fake explorers exist with one extra letter, a hyphen, or a different ending. The explorer URL you add in a wallet should be the one you intend to trust. Ads on the real explorer are not the explorer; Module 5 will repeat that.

If a “support” person sends you an RPC, a chain ID, and an explorer in one screenshot, read each field. Chain ID 56 and a lookalike explorer is still a lookalike explorer. RPC from a stranger plus chain ID 56 is still a stranger’s window onto the book.

NOTE
Academy rule: mainnet BSC is chain ID 56. RPC is a helper; random helpers can lie. Testnet is fake money — not worth local currency, not a P2P product. Your seed never belongs in an RPC field, a Discord form, or a “faster node” website.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now inspect the dropdown instead of trusting its sticker. Next: the leftover names on withdrawal screens — BEP-20, BEP-2, Beacon, opBNB — because fossils still bite.

## Say this out loud

- BNB Smart Chain mainnet is chain ID 56.
- An RPC is how a wallet talks to a node. It is not a password and not a seed.
- Testnet is a practice book with fake coins. Those coins are not worth local currency.
- Read the network chip before every signature.
- A random Discord RPC and a fake explorer are hostile until proven otherwise — and “proven” means more than a screenshot.

Next: BEP-20 versus older BEP-2 names that still confuse withdrawal screens.

lessons.title: BEP-20, BEP-2, and leftover names
lessons.content:
# BEP-20, BEP-2, and leftover names

Withdrawal screens still show fossils. Beginners lose funds not because cryptography failed, but because a dropdown said “BNB” and they did not read the help text.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to pick **BEP-20 / BSC / chain 56 / 0x** on purpose, and abort if the example address starts with bnb1 or if the label is opBNB when you meant mainnet BSC.

## BEP-20 is the token standard on this book

**BEP-20** is the token standard on **BNB Smart Chain**. It is ERC-20-style: a contract keeps a list of balances, and transfers are calls to that contract. Crystal Stones is BEP-20. USDT you want in a Trust Wallet-style 0x receive screen on BSC is BEP-20.

BEP-20 is not a coin of its own. It is a rule-set. Saying “I sent BEP-20” without naming the token is like saying “I sent a spreadsheet row” without naming the sheet.

**ERC-20** is the cousin standard on Ethereum. **BEP-20 USDT is not ERC-20 USDT.** Same sticker. Different books. Different contracts. If an exchange withdraws ERC-20 and your wallet is watching BEP-20, you will stare at an empty list and think the money died. It may be sitting on Ethereum, waiting for you to open that book, with ETH for gas, not BNB.

## BEP-2 is a leftover from an older Binance chain

**BEP-2** is an older standard on the **Beacon Chain** (the earlier Binance Chain, not the same execution environment as BSC). Addresses looked like **bnb1…**, not 0x. If you withdraw BEP-2 to an 0x wallet, pain. If you withdraw BEP-20 to a bnb1 address, pain.

Many venues have retired or renamed this. You may still see it. If you see **BEP-2 / Beacon**, that is **not** the Trust Wallet 0x receive screen from the wallets course. It is not chain 56. It is not where Crystal Stones lives as this academy references it.

Do not “try it anyway because BNB is in the name.” Names collide. Formats do not.

## “BSC”, “BEP20(BSC)”, “BNB Chain”, “opBNB”

Labels vary by venue. Read the help text, not the vibe of the word BNB.

**opBNB** is a layer-2 in the Binance family — **another book** again. Addresses may still look like 0x. That is the trap. Do not pick it because it says BNB. Pick the one that matches chain 56 mainnet, 0x destination, BEP-20 if you are moving a token.

“BNB Chain” without an info icon is ambiguous. Open the info icon. You want chain ID 56 and an 0x example. If the example starts with bnb1, abort. If it says Ethereum / ERC-20, abort. If it says Tron / TRC-20 / T-address, abort.

TABLE
Label you might see | Typical meaning | Destination shape | Is it this course’s book?
BEP20 / BSC / BNB Smart Chain | This course’s book | 0x… | Yes, if chain ID 56
ERC20 | Ethereum | 0x… (different book) | No
TRC20 | Tron | T… | No
BEP2 / Beacon | Old Binance Chain | bnb1… | No
opBNB | A different BNB-family chain | 0x… but not chain 56 | No
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** An exchange UI writes “BNB Smart Chain (BEP20).” Good. Another UI writes “BNB Chain” with no explanation.

1. Alex opens the info icon on the second UI.
2. He looks for chain ID and address format.
3. If he sees chain ID 56 and an 0x example, he proceeds with a **tiny test** first.
4. If he sees bnb1, he aborts. That is not his EVM wallet.
5. If the popup does not name chain ID or address format, he either does a shrug-able test send or picks a venue that speaks clearly. Ambiguous labels are how fossils bite.

DIAGRAM
Want tokens in an EVM wallet (MetaMask / Trust Wallet examples) on BSC
        |
        v
Need BEP-20 / BSC / chain 56 / 0x
        |
        X  not BEP-2
        X  not ERC-20
        X  not TRC-20
        X  not opBNB by accident
        X  not “BNB” as a vibe
ENDDIAGRAM

## How this bites a USDT withdrawal

The exchanges course already told you: the network dropdown on a USDT withdrawal is the whole game. This lesson names the fossils inside the Binance-family labelling.

You want USDT that will show in your BSC wallet and spend with BNB gas. That is BEP-20 USDT on chain 56. It is **not**:

- ERC-20 USDT (Ethereum; needs ETH for gas)
- TRC-20 USDT (Tron; T-addresses)
- a BEP-2 remnant
- opBNB because it was first in the list

If you already sent to the wrong book, recovery is sometimes “open the correct network with the correct native gas.” It is never “Telegram recovery admin.” Safety will labour this. Today: pick the label on purpose.

“BNB” as a withdrawal asset is a different dropdown from “USDT on BSC.” Withdrawing the native coin BNB onto chain 56 is how you get gas. Withdrawing USDT as BEP-20 is how you get the token. People pick BNB when they meant USDT, or pick a BNB-family fossil when they meant chain 56, and then say “crypto stole from me.” The dropdown stole from them. Read it twice. Send a shrug-able test.

NOTE
If the info popup does not name chain ID or address format, do a test send of a shrug-able amount or pick a venue that speaks clearly. Ambiguous labels are how fossils bite. This academy will not tell you that every withdrawal UI is well written. Some are not. That is why you read.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now treat withdrawal labels as a decoding job. Next: the 0x trap in one place, because same letters on two books still deserve their own lesson.

## Say this out loud

- BEP-20 means tokens on BNB Smart Chain, 0x addresses, chain 56.
- BEP-2 is an old chain with bnb1 addresses — not your EVM wallet.
- BEP-20 USDT is not ERC-20 USDT. Same sticker, different book, different contract.
- opBNB is another book. Do not pick it because it says BNB.
- Read the info icon for chain ID and address format, not the vibe of the word BNB.

Next: the 0x trap on two books — same letters, different planet.

lessons.title: The 0x address trap on two books
lessons.content:
# The 0x address trap on two books

Your seed on an EVM wallet can produce the **same 0x text** for Ethereum and for BNB Smart Chain. That is convenient. It is also the expensive confusion that sits right behind “USDT is USDT.”

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say: same letters, different planet; network first, then copy, then withdraw; recovery is “open the other book,” not “send a seed to support.”

## Same key, two ledgers

The private key signs EVM transactions. The **chain ID** inside the signed message says which book. Balances:

- ETH and ERC-20 tokens live on Ethereum
- BNB and BEP-20 tokens live on BSC
- they do **not** add up

You can be funded on one and empty on the other with the same letters in the receive box. The wallet app is a window. Switching the dropdown changes the window. It does not merge the piles.

This is not a bug in “the blockchain.” It is two books sharing a key format because they share an engine family. Shared format is not shared money.

## How to not mix them

Ritual, in this order:

1. Set the wallet **network** first. For this academy’s practice, BSC — chain ID 56.
2. Copy the receive address **after** the chip is right. (The letters may look the same anyway. The chip is for you, not for the alphabet.)
3. Set the exchange withdrawal to that **same** network. BEP-20 / BSC, not ERC-20, not TRC-20.
4. Send a tiny test. Confirm on the explorer of that network. BscScan for BSC. Etherscan for Ethereum.
5. Only then send the rest.

If you skip step 1, you will still copy a valid-looking 0x. Validity of letters is not validity of book.

## If you already mixed them

If you sent ERC-20 to your 0x and your BSC wallet shows 0, look at **Etherscan**, not only BscScan. If you sent BEP-20 and Etherscan is empty, look at BscScan. If both explorers are empty, it may not have left the exchange, or the hash is wrong, or it is still pending.

You may still control the key that owns the other book. Recovery is: open the **correct network** in a wallet that can speak it, with the **native gas of that network** (ETH on Ethereum, BNB on BSC). It is not: a Telegram recovery bot. It is not: a “cross-chain unstucker” that wants a seed. It is not: bridging through a sponsored tweet.

If the destination was a contract that only exists on one chain, or an exchange deposit address tagged for one network, recovery may be a support ticket at that venue — slow, sometimes impossible — not a miracle dApp.

TABLE
Symptom | Likely reality | First honest move
Sent ERC-20 to 0x, wallet on BSC shows 0 | Funds may be on Ethereum | Check Etherscan; you need ETH to move them
Sent BEP-20, Etherscan empty | Funds may be on BSC | Check BscScan; you need BNB to move them
Both explorers empty | Not included yet, never left the CEX, or wrong hash | Check the venue’s withdrawal history and the hash
A helper wants a seed to “merge the chains” | Theft | Close the chat
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Sam sends USDT BEP-20 correctly to her wallet. Then she sends “the same” USDT to the same 0x from another venue but leaves that venue on ERC-20.

1. She now has two piles on two books.
2. She only watches BscScan. She thinks half vanished.
3. A group admin says “same address so it must be there, send 0.1 BNB to this helper to unlock the hidden ERC-20.”
4. She refuses. She opens Etherscan. The ERC-20 USDT is there.
5. Two books, one string. She will need ETH as gas on Ethereum if she wants to move that pile. She will not send BNB to a stranger to “unlock” Ethereum.

DIAGRAM
Seed --> same 0x string
          |
          +--> Ethereum balances (ETH, ERC-20)   --> Etherscan
          +--> BSC balances (BNB, BEP-20)        --> BscScan

Watch BOTH explorers if you used BOTH networks.
Better: use one network on purpose.
This academy’s default practice network is BSC.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Prefer one practice network

This academy’s default practice network is BSC. Pick it on purpose every time rather than “whichever the dropdown remembered.” One practice network means one explorer, one gas coin, one withdrawal label. That is how you get reps without collecting recovery stories.

When you later need Ethereum for some other reason, you will treat it as a second book with a second gas coin, not as “the same wallet so the same money.”

Copy-paste still bites even when the network is right. Messaging apps insert invisible characters. A trailing space can break a checksum. Paste into the wallet, look at the first six and last four characters out loud, compare to the explorer or the paper you already checked. If a cousin reads the address over a phone call, they will get one character wrong. Do not take addresses by voice.

NOTE
Academy rule: same 0x, different books, different balances. Network first, then copy, then withdraw. Recovery is “open the other book with that book’s native gas,” not “send a seed to support.” Prefer one practice network so you are not always on both planets at once.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The 0x trap now has its own shelf in your head. Next: native coin versus token — BNB as fuel and value, tokens as rows in contracts, and why sending BNB to a token contract is not a purchase.

## Say this out loud

- Same 0x letters on Ethereum and BSC do not mean the same account-as-balance. The key can speak both books; the money is not shared.
- Network first, then copy the address, then set the withdrawal to that same network.
- If you mixed books, open the explorer for the book you actually sent on. Do not send a seed to a recovery admin.
- BEP-20 USDT is not ERC-20 USDT even when the receive letters match.
- Prefer one practice network. This academy’s is BSC, chain ID 56.

Next: native coin versus token — fuel versus rows in a contract.

lessons.title: Native coin versus token
lessons.content:
# Native coin versus token

On BNB Smart Chain there is one **native** asset — **BNB** — and a universe of **tokens** implemented as contracts. Mixing those two objects is how people “deposit to the contract to mint” and light their gas on fire.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say where BNB lives, where Crystal Stones lives, and why your wallet address is the pocket while the token contract is the rule-book.

## Native: the chain’s own coin

**BNB** on BSC is native. That means:

- it is not a BEP-20
- it pays **gas**
- it appears as **value** on a simple send
- the chain’s existence does not depend on a single token contract

You can send BNB to a friend’s 0x the way you send a native payment: **to** is the friend, **value** is the amount. You still pay a little extra BNB as the fee. If you try to empty the tank to zero in one send, the wallet may refuse, because the fee has to come from somewhere.

Without BNB, you can **see** tokens and you cannot **move** them. Holding a large BEP-20 balance with 0 BNB is like having inventory in a locked shop. The book shows the inventory. The door needs fuel.

## Token: a row in a contract’s list

A **token** on BSC is a **contract** — a program plus storage — that keeps a list: address → balance. When you “hold Crystal Stones,” you are an entry in that contract’s mapping. The contract, as this academy references the project, is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. That sentence is verification geography. It is not a buy order.

USDT as BEP-20 is the same shape: a different contract, a different list. The sticker “USDT” is also used on Ethereum and Tron. The list is not shared.

If you sent BNB to the token **contract** by mistake (as native value), you may have gifted the program, not “converted.” Token contracts are not shop tills that automatically swap native coin into the ticker. Some contracts have functions that accept BNB. Many do not send it back to strangers. “Deposit to the contract to mint” from a YouTube comment is how people donate.

## Your wallet address holds both; the contract address is not your pocket

Your **wallet address** (an externally owned account) can show:

- BNB (native)
- USDT according to the USDT contract
- Crystal Stones according to the Crystal Stones contract
- a pile of spam tokens you never asked for

The **token contract address** is the program. It is not a deposit box with your name on it. You interact with it by sending a transaction that calls a function — transfer, approve, and later, if you ever use a DEX, a router. You do not mail native BNB into it as if it were a person named Crystal.

TABLE
Action | Result
Send BNB to a friend’s 0x | Friend can spend BNB (after inclusion)
Send BNB to a token contract address as value | Often stuck; not a swap; not a purchase
Send token via the contract’s transfer | Friend’s token balance updates
Hold token with 0 BNB | You can see it; you cannot move it
Add a token to the wallet display | A sticker on the window; coins do not move
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student wants Crystal Stones. A YouTube comment says “deposit BNB to the contract to mint.”

1. They withdraw BNB from an exchange **to the Crystal Stones contract address**.
2. BscScan shows a native BNB send **to** the contract. Token transfers do not show a mint to them.
3. The contract did not mint them a gift. They sent native BNB into a program that does not have a withdraw-for-strangers button.
4. Correct pattern, if they ever buy at all — this course does not require it — is a centralised exchange trade, or later a DEX swap they understand. Not mailing fuel into a program.
5. Correct pattern for holding: BNB and tokens **in your wallet address**. Interact only through known functions.

DIAGRAM
Your wallet address (the pocket)
   - BNB (fuel + native value)
   - USDT contract says you have X
   - Crystal Stones contract says you have Y

The token contract address (the rule-book)
   - keeps the list
   - is NOT your piggy-bank deposit box
   - mailing BNB into it is not a purchase
ENDDIAGRAM

## This academy will not tell you to buy

You can finish this course, including the labs, without purchasing Crystal Stones, USDT, or extra BNB beyond a tiny gas practice if you even do that. Verifying a contract is literacy. Adding a token to a display is literacy. Neither is a market order.

RWA claims around Crystal Stones — minerals, vaults, backing — are **project claims to verify** in the legal and audit world. They are not classroom proof that a vault exists. A BEP-20 balance is a row in a contract. A row in a contract is not a gold bar in your hand.

NOTE
Never “send tokens to the contract to buy.” Buying, if you ever do it, is a DEX swap or a CEX trade — different skills, later or optional. Sending native BNB into a random contract as if it were a person is a classic loss. This classroom is still not a buy order.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Native versus token is now a reflex. Last lesson of this module: what it actually means when a wallet “adds BSC.” You are pointing a window at a book, not installing a new universe.

## Say this out loud

- BNB is native on BSC. It pays gas and can be sent as value. Tokens are rows in contracts.
- Your wallet address is the pocket. The token contract is the rule-book, not a deposit box.
- Holding a token with 0 BNB means you can see it and you cannot move it.
- Sending native BNB into a token contract is not a purchase and often sticks.
- Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 row, not native gas, and verifying its contract is not a buy order.

Next: how a wallet “adds BSC” — you are pointing the window at a book.

lessons.title: How a wallet “adds BSC”
lessons.content:
# How a wallet “adds BSC”

When a wallet “adds a network,” you are not downloading a chain into the phone. You are pointing the window at a book: RPC, chain ID, native symbol, explorer. The book was already there. Your seed, if it is an EVM seed, could already speak that book. The dropdown was just looking at a different one.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to add BSC on purpose — chain ID 56 — and refuse a dApp popup that fills a lookalike RPC.

## You are pointing the window, not installing a universe

A wallet app is a key manager plus a picture of whatever book you pointed it at. **Add network** fills in:

- a human name (“BNB Smart Chain”)
- an **RPC** URL (the counter)
- **chain ID 56**
- native currency symbol **BNB**
- an explorer URL, which should be https://bscscan.com if that is the window you intend

If chain ID is wrong, stop. If someone wants you to scan a QR that fills an RPC you cannot read, stop. If the explorer field is a lookalike, stop. The name can be honest while the RPC is a liar.

Trust Wallet often has BSC built in. MetaMask may need Add network. Both are **examples of wallet apps**, not endorsements. Built-in is still a window. Confirm the chip before you sign.

## The fields, again, as a checklist

When you add by hand, read every line:

- Network name: can be fake; the number matters more
- RPC: known public endpoint, or the wallet’s own suggestion, not a Discord gift
- Chain ID: **56**
- Currency: BNB
- Explorer: https://bscscan.com

Chain ID is the line that stops replay across books. If a form says 56 but the RPC hostname is a lookalike of a known host, cancel and add from the wallet’s own list or from documentation you already trust.

## Built-in versus custom versus dApp popup

Three doors, different manners:

- **Built-in BSC** — still confirm you are on it before signing. Dropdowns drift.
- **Custom network form** — you type the fields. Slow. Honest if you type honestly.
- **“Add network” popup from a dApp** — the site suggests fields. Convenient. Also how a trap chain gets installed with a friendly name.

A dApp can suggest chain ID 56 and a hostile RPC. A dApp can suggest a friendly name and chain ID something-else. Read. You are not being rude. You are doing the job.

TABLE
Wallet behaviour | Your job
Built-in BSC | Still confirm you are on it before signing
Custom network form | Chain ID 56, known RPC, known explorer
“Add network” popup from a dApp | Read fields; dApps can suggest a trap chain
QR from a stranger that “auto-fills BSC” | Do not scan
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A dApp pops “Add Binance Smart Chain” with chain ID 56 but an RPC hostname that is a lookalike.

1. The student does not tap Approve because the name looks right.
2. They cancel the popup.
3. They add BSC from MetaMask’s own list, or from documentation they already trust, checking chain ID 56 and bscscan.com.
4. Extra thirty seconds. Fewer surprises.
5. They still read the network chip before every later signature, because adding the network once is not a blessing that lasts if they switch to Ethereum and forget.

DIAGRAM
Need BSC
  --> wallet’s built-in or documented add
  --> chain ID 56
  --> known RPC
  --> explorer bscscan.com
  X  not a popup from a sponsored dApp you just met
  X  not a QR in a WhatsApp status
  X  not “BSC Ultra” with a new ID
ENDDIAGRAM

## Multiple networks in one seed is normal and dangerous

You can hold BSC, Ethereum, and others behind one seed. That is normal EVM life. It increases the number of ways to pick the wrong dropdown. For this academy, keep the chip on BSC when you mean BSC.

Adding a network does not make a fake app honest. The wallets course covered clones. It still applies. Official store, official app. Adding BSC on a fake APK gives a thief a window and a key.

You do not need ten wallets. One official software wallet for practice, later hardware for amounts you would miss. More apps is more clone surface.

Adding BSC does not give you BNB. The window can be aimed perfectly at chain 56 and still show 0. That is not a broken add. That is an empty fuel gauge. People “add BSC” and then rage that Crystal Stones will not send. They needed native BNB on that address, not a second copy of the network form. Do not pay a site that claims to “activate BSC” after you added it. Activation is a scam word. The book does not need a blessing. It needs a signed transaction and a fee in BNB if you want to write. Reading needs even less: BscScan already reads without the wallet.

If you add BSC twice with two RPCs, you may see two entries that look like twins. Delete the one with the stranger’s URL. Keep chain ID 56 and the explorer you intended. Twins are how people later sign on a liar window that still says “BNB Smart Chain” at the top.

NOTE
Academy rule: adding BSC is pointing a window at chain ID 56. It is not a purchase, not a node, and not a reason to scan a stranger’s QR. Prefer the wallet’s built-in or documented network list. dApp popups are suggestions, not commands.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 2 is a specific book: why it exists, its numbers, its leftover names, its 0x trap, its native coin, and how a wallet aims at it. Module 3 puts tokens and the Crystal Stones contract under the light — as literacy, not a pitch.

## Say this out loud

- Adding BSC means pointing the wallet’s window at chain ID 56, a known RPC, symbol BNB, explorer bscscan.com.
- The book was already there. You did not install a universe.
- dApp “add network” popups are suggestions. Read the chain ID and the RPC.
- One honest wallet beats five random APKs.
- The network chip is part of every send, even after you added the network once.

Take the quiz. Module 3: tokens, contracts, and Crystal Stones as a case — verify, do not buy.
