lessons.title: What a contract address is
lessons.content:
# What a contract address is

An EVM address is 20 bytes, shown as 0x plus 40 hex characters. Two important kinds live in that same clothing: a person’s key, and a program. Mixing them is how names become traps.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say that **address is identity**, **name is a sticker**, and the Crystal Stones contract this academy references is a string to verify, not a buy order.

## Externally owned versus contract

An **externally owned account (EOA)** is a person or wallet, controlled by a key. Your Trust Wallet or MetaMask receive address is this. If the key signs, the account spends.

A **contract** is code deployed on-chain. No seed. It does what its bytecode and its owner permissions allow. You cannot “log in” to a contract with a password. You call functions by sending transactions.

Both look like 0x plus forty characters. The explorer will usually label a contract as a contract. Your job is to notice the label. Sending native BNB to a contract as if it were your cousin is Module 2’s failure mode. Sending tokens to a lookalike contract because the name matched is this module’s.

## Why the string matters more than the name

Anyone can deploy a contract and call it Crystal Stones, USDT, or BNB2. The **address** is the identity. Names in wallets are stickers. Logos are stickers. Telegram titles are stickers.

Crystal Stones, as this academy references the project:

**0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**

on BNB Smart Chain. Save it from a source you trust — the project’s long-standing site and official channels you already verified, not a Google ad, not a WhatsApp status. Compare character by character when you add a token.

This classroom does not certify that the project’s mineral story is true. RWA claims are **project claims to verify**. A contract address is only the on-chain object those claims point at. Verifying the pointer is not a purchase and not a vault tour.

## Checksum is a stop sign

Some letters are uppercase on purpose (**EIP-55 checksum**). The mix of upper and lower case is a built-in typo check. If you paste and the wallet warns about checksum, stop and re-copy. It may be a typo. One wrong character is a different person or a different program — often a black hole.

Do not “fix” the address from memory. Do not accept a helper’s version with two characters different “because of formatting.” Copy, paste, compare.

Contracts can also be **proxies**: one address you see, another address that holds the logic. Explorers sometimes show “Read as Proxy.” That is Intermediate. Today you only need: the address you paste is still the identity of the token you mean. A helper who says “use this implementation address instead, the other one is outdated” is often handing you a clone. Stay with the token address the project published and that BscScan’s token tracker uses for transfers.

Creating a contract is cheap. That is why identity cannot be a vibe. The next lessons will show you clones that look more official than the real tracker. Your defence starts here: the string, checksum, more than one source.

TABLE
Object | Controlled by | Example job | Identity
EOA | Private key / seed | Your pocket | The 0x your wallet shows
Token contract | Its code, plus owner keys if the code allows | Balances of a ticker | The 0x of the program
DEX router | Its code | Swaps | A different 0x; not the token
Explorer page | A website | A view | A URL; not the contract itself
Name / logo | Whoever deployed or whoever designed a sticker | Marketing | Not identity
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Two BscScan pages: the real Crystal Stones contract, and a clone created yesterday with extra supply and a similar name.

1. Wallet search by name shows both. The clone may even sit higher if someone paid to spam it.
2. A student who adds via an airdrop popup gets the clone. Their “balance” is a row in the wrong list.
3. A student who pastes 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 from a source they already verified gets one contract.
4. They still might not buy. This course does not require it. They refused a fake.
5. If a checksum warning appears, they stop and re-copy rather than ignoring the yellow text.

DIAGRAM
Name sticker  -->  many possible contracts
Logo          -->  many possible contracts
Address       -->  one contract on that chain

Always add by address from a verified source.
Verifying is not a buy order.
ENDDIAGRAM

## You will meet this string again

You will paste it in the token-page lesson, in the add-token lesson, and in Module 6’s lab. Repetition is the point. Scammers win on the day you are tired and search by name.

Write it in your own notes, from a source you trust, and compare. Do not trust this paragraph alone if you are about to move funds — open the project’s long-standing site as well, and confirm the explorer. Multiple sources. Module 6 will make that a lab.

NOTE
This lesson is still not a buy order. It is how you refuse fakes if you later look at a token at all. Academy staff will not DM you a “new contract.” A surprise migration is hostile until a slow public verification exists.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Identity is now a string. Next: a guided look at the Crystal Stones page on BscScan — holders, transfers, contract tab — as literacy, not a pitch.

## Say this out loud

- Address is identity. Name and logo are stickers.
- An EOA is controlled by a key. A contract is code, with no seed to “log in.”
- Crystal Stones, as this academy references it, is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on BSC — verify, do not treat that as a buy.
- Checksum warnings are stop signs. Do not improve an address from memory.
- Add tokens by contract from a source you already verified, not by a popup’s name.

Next: a guided look at the Crystal Stones token page on BscScan.

lessons.title: Reading the Crystal Stones token page on BscScan
lessons.content:
# Reading the Crystal Stones token page on BscScan

Open BscScan from a bookmark, not from a chat link. Paste:

**0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**

You should land on a **contract / token** page on the real domain. Check the domain character by character. This lesson is literacy. It is not a pitch. This academy will not tell you to buy.

By the end you should know what holders, transfers, and the contract tab are for, and you should know that a **verified** contract is not a safe investment.

## Domain first, then the sticker

Fake explorers exist. Ads on the real explorer exist. If the page asks you to **connect a wallet to view** a public balance, you are probably not on BscScan. Public balances do not need your seed.

**Contract / token name and symbol** are stickers. Confirm they match what the project publishes. Clones will also set pretty stickers. The address is still the identity.

## Decimals and total supply are mechanical, not a price

**Decimals** say how many places the token uses to display. The chain stores integers. Wallets hide this. Display bugs happen when a wallet assumes 18 and the token uses 9, or the reverse. Confirm amounts on the explorer’s token-transfer row, which usually formats with the token’s own decimals.

**Total supply** is how many units the contract says exist (in display terms). This is **not** market cap, not price, not “backed by a vault.” It is a number in a program. Tokenomics as a subject is later. Today: know the number is a contract fact, and a PDF that disagrees with the contract is a PDF.

## Holders and transfers are history, not a promise

**Holders** is the list of who has a balance. Huge concentration in a few addresses can matter later. Today: know the tab exists. Do not harass holders in DMs. A big holder is not a promise of price, of vaults, or of your future. Module 5 will labour this.

**Transfers** is the living history of the token. This is how you verify “someone paid me Crystal Stones.” Filter the contract, read from, to, amount, status. A group screenshot is not this tab.

If a group claims “the team dumped,” this tab is where you look — and you may still not know whether a move was a DEX swap, a CEX deposit, or a lie. Looking is the skill. Repeating a caption is not.

## Contract tab: verified is hygiene, not a blessing

If BscScan shows **verified** source code, the published source matches the bytecode the chain is running. Unverified means you are trusting a black box. Verification is good hygiene. It is not a halo.

**Verified scam contracts exist.** People publish readable code that still lets them pause you, mint on you, or trap a sale. “Verified” means “you can read what it does if you can read it.” It does not mean “safe investment.” It does not mean “the mineral vault is real.” It does not mean this academy tells you to buy.

**Read contract** lets you read public numbers without connecting a wallet. **Write contract** is a way to send transactions through the explorer. Do **not** write — especially owner functions — because a YouTube comment said to. Connecting a wallet to BscScan write is still connecting a wallet.

TABLE
Tab | Beginner use | Not a license for
Name / symbol | Compare to the project’s published sticker | Trusting a clone with a prettier logo
Decimals / supply | Mechanical display and a contract number | Price targets
Holders | Curiosity about concentration | A target list, a promise, a vault proof
Transfers | Did a payment happen? | Ignoring the contract address
Contract (verified?) | Hygiene: can the source be matched to bytecode? | “Verified = safe investment”
Read | Numbers without signing | None — this is the safe tab
Write | Usually not for you today | Owner clicks because a comment said so
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A group claims “the team dumped Crystal Stones, it is over.”

1. Maya does not reshare the caption. She opens BscScan from a bookmark.
2. She pastes 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Domain is real. Address matches.
3. She opens Transfers. She looks at large recent moves. She does not yet know what each address is.
4. She notices that a pretty caption is not a from/to/amount/status row. Sometimes the story is a DEX hop. Sometimes it is a CEX deposit. Sometimes it is a lie.
5. She still does not buy or sell because a classroom said to. She learned to look. She closes the tab without connecting a wallet.

DIAGRAM
BscScan token page (real domain)
   Transfers  -->  payments
   Holders    -->  concentration, not a promise
   Contract   -->  verified code / owner — hygiene, not a blessing
   Read       -->  numbers without signing
   Write      -->  not your beginner tool
   Ads        -->  not the product; never connect from a banner
ENDDIAGRAM

## RWA claims are not this page

crystalstones.org may describe minerals, supply figures, taxes, burns. Those are **website / whitepaper parameters**. This BscScan page shows the on-chain object: transfers, holders, code status. A classroom paragraph is not a receipt for a vault. A receipt would be legal title, custody, and audit you can follow. We will not invent that receipt.

NOTE
If the page asks you to connect a wallet to **view** a balance, you are probably not on BscScan. Public balances do not need your seed. Verified source is not a safe-investment stamp. This academy will not tell you to buy because a contract tab is green.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can walk a token page without being sold to. Next: clones, similar names, and fake liquidity — because the search box is hostile.

## Say this out loud

- The Crystal Stones token page is identity plus history plus code status, not a shop window.
- Supply is a contract number, not a price and not proof of a vault.
- Transfers settle payment arguments. Holders are not a promise.
- A verified contract means the source matches bytecode. It does not mean a safe investment.
- Connect-wallet to “view” is a red flag on an explorer clone.

Next: clones, similar names, and fake liquidity.

lessons.title: Clones, similar names, and fake liquidity
lessons.content:
# Clones, similar names, and fake liquidity

Creating a BEP-20 is cheap. Creating a pool with a stolen logo is cheap. The industry calls them **scam tokens**, **honeypots**, **clones**. You will meet them the moment you search a name.

By the end of this lesson you should refuse name search, refuse surprise “migration” DMs, and treat a pretty chart as theatre until you know which contract you are looking at.

## Cheap to deploy is the whole problem

Anyone with a little BNB can deploy a contract and name it Crystal Stones, USDT, or Tesla. The chain will accept the deployment because the chain does not parent you. The book records the program. The book does not certify the sticker.

That is why this academy repeats the address. **0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**. Extra spaces, Cyrillic letters, “Crystal Stone” singular, “Crystal Stones 2.0,” “official Crystal Stones v3” — different objects. Some will even show a prettier chart than the real one, because painting a chart is cheap too.

## Honeypot, in beginner language

A **honeypot** is a contract that lets you buy but not sell, or takes a ruinous fee on exit, or blacklists the buyer. The chart only goes up on the way in. You are not a trader. You are the exit liquidity of nobody.

You do not need to be a contract reader to take the beginner precaution: **do not buy a token you found by name search.** If you cannot explain which contract you are interacting with, you are not investing. You are volunteering.

This course will not teach you how to launch a token so you can be on the other side of that chart. Advanced is not Basic, and it is not a side hustle we will sell you in a footnote.

Liquidity captions deserve the same coldness. “Locked LP,” “burned LP,” “huge liquidity” are words. Intermediate will ask which locker contract, until when, and whether the lock is even of the pair you think. Basic’s version: a clone can show a pool with stolen logos and a number that looks like money. If you cannot paste the token contract and the pair contract into BscScan yourself, you do not have liquidity. You have a graphic.

Fake volume is the sibling. A bot can buy and sell with itself. A chart can go up and to the right on a token nobody else can exit. “Daily volume” on a name-search result is not a reason to paste an unknown address into a swap. It is a reason to close the tab.

## Name search is hostile; fake volume is theatre

Trust Wallet’s add-token search, PancakeSwap search, Gecko-style sites — they index **many** contracts. Ranking is not holiness. Ranking can be spam, paid placement, or volume painted by a bot loop.

Tiny buys in a loop can paint a chart. If you cannot see **who** is trading and whether sells succeed for strangers, you do not have a market. You have theatre. “Liquidity” in a caption is not the same as a pool you can exit.

TABLE
Check | Why | Beginner action
Address match | Identity | Paste the known contract; ignore the rest
Name search | Hostile index | Do not use it to pick what to hold
Pretty chart | Can be painted | Not sellability
Born-yesterday + huge APR | Smell | Walk away
Surprise migration DM | Clone attempt | Treat as hostile
“Add this new contract tonight” | Classic drain setup | Academy staff will not do this
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Search “Crystal Stones” on a DEX aggregator. Five results. One address matches. Four do not. The four may even show a prettier chart.

1. The student only opens the matching address: 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
2. They still might not buy — this course does not require it — but they did not buy a trap.
3. A DM arrives: “we migrated, add this new contract tonight, old one is dead.”
4. They treat it as hostile. Migrations, if they ever happened, would be a public, slow, verifiable event — not a Friday night surprise.
5. They do not approve a spender “to migrate.” They do not send BNB to a helper.

DIAGRAM
Search by name  -->  a pile of lookalikes
Paste address   -->  one contract
Chart without identity --> theatre
Surprise migration DM --> clone attempt

If you will ever interact, paste.
If you will not interact, you still learned to refuse.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Academy staff will not migrate you in a chat

Write this until it is boring: Crystal Stones Academy staff never ask for seed phrase, private key, 2FA codes, or remote screen control. They also will not send you a “new contract because we migrated, add this now” in a DM.

If a real migration ever existed, you would verify it the slow way: official long-standing site, explorer, more than one source, time to think. Basic does not ask you to migrate anything.

NOTE
Cheap to clone a name. Expensive to undo a buy. Search by address. Pretty chart is not sellability. Surprise “migration” DMs are hostile. This classroom is still not a buy order for the real contract either.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now treat the search box as an adversary. Next: decimals, supply, and what tokenomics is not — so a PDF cannot outshout a contract.

## Say this out loud

- Creating a BEP-20 with a stolen name is cheap. That is why address is identity.
- A honeypot lets you buy and then blocks or wrecks selling. Name search is how people walk in.
- Pretty charts can be painted. They are not proof you can exit.
- Surprise migration DMs are hostile. Academy staff will not send you a new contract on a Friday night.
- Paste the known address. This academy will not tell you to buy it.

Next: decimals, supply, and the tokenomics claims you should not swallow yet.

lessons.title: Decimals, supply, and what tokenomics is not
lessons.content:
# Decimals, supply, and what tokenomics is not

People quote “billion supply” or “only 1 million” as if that were price. **Price × supply** fantasies belong later. Today, mechanical facts: how wallets display integers, what total supply actually is, and why a PDF is not bytecode.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to refuse a rocket-emoji tokenomics page as a substitute for the contract, and you should know that decimals are a display rule, not a local currency price.

## Decimals are a display rule

If **decimals** = 18, one display token is 10^18 base units in the contract. Wallets hide this. You see “1.0.” The chain sees a giant integer.

Bugs: a site shows 0.000000000000000001 as “you received 1.” Another site shows 1 as “you received 0.000000000000000001.” Always confirm amount on BscScan’s token transfer, which usually formats with the token’s decimals.

Decimals do not set the local currency price. They do not hide the owner. They do not replace gas. They tell wallets how to place a decimal point. If a helper says “your decimals are locked, send BNB to unlock,” they are stealing.

## Supply is a contract number; mint is a capability

**Total supply** can be fixed or mintable. If the contract owner can **mint**, they can create more tokens. That is not automatically evil — some designs need it — and not automatically fine — it can dilute holders. Read whether mint is possible only if you later care about holding. BscScan’s Read functions often expose owner and totalSupply without a signature.

A PDF that says “max supply 100 million” is a **policy**. A mint function that still exists is a **capability**. Capabilities beat PDFs when they disagree. The next lesson is the full decentralisation test: admin keys, pause, mint. Today, park this sentence: **the chain describes what the program can do, not what a designer hopes they will do.**

## What tokenomics is not

**Tokenomics** means, in later courses: how tokens are created, allocated, released, taxed, and used. You cannot audit that from a sticker pack.

Tokenomics is not:

- a guarantee of price
- a reason to skip the contract address
- a PDF with a rocket emoji
- “2% reflections” as a job replacement
- classroom proof that a mineral vault exists
- a reason this academy tells you to buy

Crystal Stones’ deeper economics belong in a later ecosystem course if you ever take it. Basic only trains you not to confuse a PDF with bytecode.

TABLE
Claim in a PDF | Mechanical question | Who wins if they disagree
“Limited supply” | Can owner mint? Is there a hidden mint role? | The contract’s capability
“LP locked” | Locked where, until when, which locker contract? | The locker, if it is real — later skill
“Renounced” | Owner is zero — also means bugs cannot be patched | Explorer owner field, not the caption
“Audited” | By whom, which commit, paid by whom? | Scope of the audit, not the badge
“RWA backed” | Legal title, custody, audit you can follow? | Not a classroom paragraph
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A PDF says max supply 100 million. BscScan totalSupply is 100 million today. An owner mint function still exists.

1. A student quotes the PDF in a group as “proof the supply cannot grow.”
2. Another student opens Read contract, or at least remembers this lesson: capability versus policy.
3. They do not need to be developers. They need the question: **can someone still mint?**
4. If yes, the PDF described a hope. The chain described a button.
5. They still do not have a buy or sell order from this classroom. They have a better question.

DIAGRAM
PDF / Telegram  -->  marketing (policy, hope, story)
Contract code   -->  capabilities (mint, pause, tax, owner)
Price chart     -->  yesterday’s trades (not tomorrow)
RWA brochure    -->  claims to verify in the legal world

Do not mix the four.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Display bugs are not theft, and theft is not a display bug

If the wallet shows a strange amount, check the explorer before you panic-send a “correction” or click a “fix decimals” site. If the explorer shows the amount you expected, the wallet display is late or wrong. If the explorer shows 0, you were not paid in that contract — clone, pending, or never sent.

Do not let a display bug bounce you into a helper. Helpers who fix decimals want keys.

A “billion supply” scare and a “only 1 million” brag can describe the same human wealth if the price is different. That is why Basic will not let you use supply as a personality test. You are allowed to notice mint capability. You are not required to compute a fully diluted local currency figure in this course. Anyone selling you a target from a supply slide is doing marketing. Marketing is not consensus. Crystal Mentor, when you use it, must refuse investment instructions. So must this page.

Taxes and burns, if a project claims them, are also mechanical only when they actually execute on transfers. A PDF can say 2% forever. A contract can let an admin change the tax. Capability versus policy, again. Intermediate can read those functions. You can already refuse the PDF as bytecode.

NOTE
Crystal Stones’ deeper economics belong in a later course. Basic only trains you not to confuse a PDF with bytecode. RWA numbers on a website are not explorer facts. This academy will not repeat market-cap targets as if they were consensus.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Mechanical numbers now have a shelf. Next: the decentralisation test from Foundations, reused on this book — admin keys, pause, mint — without turning you into a Solidity reader.

## Say this out loud

- Decimals tell wallets how to display integer base units. They are not a local currency price.
- Total supply is a contract number. If mint still exists, a PDF’s “limited supply” is a policy, not a lock.
- Tokenomics is a later subject. A rocket PDF is not bytecode.
- RWA backing is a claim to verify, not a classroom receipt for a vault.
- Confirm amounts on BscScan’s token transfer, not on a site that wants to “fix decimals.”

Next: admin keys, pause, mint — the decentralisation test reused from Foundations.

lessons.title: Admin keys, pause, mint — the decentralisation test
lessons.content:
# Admin keys, pause, mint — the decentralisation test

Foundations already gave you a test for the most abused word in crypto: **decentralised**. This lesson reuses it on BNB Smart Chain tokens, including Crystal Stones as a case you inspect, not a case you are told to buy.

By the end you should be able to ask who can mint, who can pause, and who you must trust, without reading Solidity for a living.

## Decentralised is a test of power, not a vibe

In this academy it has a testable meaning: **no single office can unilaterally rewrite the ledger, freeze every user, or change the rules without the network noticing.**

A token can sit on a public chain and still be a company product. BSC can be a public book — with a concentrated validator set, as Module 1 said — and a BEP-20 on it can still have an **admin key**. Those layers stack. Slogans smash them.

An **admin key** means a privileged secret the deployer kept so they can mint, pause, blacklist, change taxes, or upgrade. It is not automatically evil. It is automatically power. Power should be named.

## The five questions, now with a token page

When a site says decentralised, ask, slowly:

1. Can I verify the contract address from more than the project’s banner?
2. Can the team **pause** transfers?
3. Can they **mint** extra tokens?
4. Can they pull the trading pool (a **rug** — they yank the money and leave you holding a name)?
5. If the website dies, does the token still exist on the chain?

For Crystal Stones, the public BEP-20 this academy references is still 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Treat that as a **reference to verify**, not a request to buy. Always check the address on a block explorer yourself.

You may not yet be able to answer questions 2–4 from source code. You can still look at BscScan’s contract tab, owner field, and project documentation, and you can still refuse a slogan that will not survive the questions. Intermediate will do contracts for real. Basic gives you the questions so you are not helpless in a Telegram argument.

## Pause, mint, blacklist, upgrade, renounce

**Pause** means an admin can stop transfers. Useful in an emergency. Also a freeze button.

**Mint** means new units can be created. Useful in some designs. Also a private printer.

**Blacklist** means selected addresses cannot move the token. Useful against thieves, in the team’s story. Also a way to trap you.

**Upgrade** means the code can be swapped. A company product with a patch cycle. Do not call it unchangeable.

**Renounced** means the owner was set to a zero address — the team gave up the admin keys, if that is actually true on-chain. That can be safer against silent minting and also **unable to fix a bug**. Renounce is not a halo. An audit is not a halo. Audits have **scope**. They are not insurance.

TABLE
Power | What it can do | Honest sentence
Mint | Create more tokens | “Supply can grow if this role exists”
Pause | Stop transfers | “They can freeze movement”
Blacklist | Block selected addresses | “Some holders can be trapped”
Upgrade | Swap the code | “This is a product, not a stone tablet”
Renounce | Drop the owner key | “They cannot patch; they also cannot quietly mint — if it is real”
Audit badge | A report with a scope | “Someone checked some things, paid by someone”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A website says “fully decentralized token.” You ask five questions and get: the team can pause transfers, they can mint, liquidity sits in a pool they can empty, and the only market is their own site.

1. The chain underneath may still be public. BSC still seals pages.
2. The *product* is not decentralised. You have used the layer test.
3. You do not need to argue in caps. You name the powers.
4. If the product is Crystal Stones, you still verify the contract, and you still treat RWA vault stories as claims, not as this classroom’s proof.
5. You do not send a seed to a stranger who promises to “decentralise your wallet.” That sentence is theft.

DIAGRAM
Someone says “we are decentralized”
                 |
     ----------------------------
     |            |             |
 Open public    Team can still   You still need
 chain (BSC)    mint, pause,     a wallet, an
                or upgrade       app, an exchange

Ask the five questions. Do not stop at the sticker.
ENDDIAGRAM

## RWA does not skip the test

A real-world-asset story says the token points at off-chain things. That claim lives in the legal and audit world. It does **not** turn an admin key into a halo. It does **not** make a clone safe. It does **not** make this classroom a vault inspector.

If the website dies, a BEP-20 can still exist on BSC as a list of balances. That is the chain layer. Whether anyone will buy those balances, and whether a mineral title exists, are different layers. Keep them separate and you cannot be slogan-bullied.

NOTE
Holding the secret that controls coins is power and liability. A “decentralised” token sitting inside a centralised exchange account is, for practical purposes, an IOU from that exchange. Admin keys on the token are a different office of power. Name both. This academy will not tell you to buy because a page says renounced, audited, or RWA.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You reused Foundations’ test on this book. Last lesson of the module: adding a token by contract so the icon appears without a trap, and without imagining that adding is buying.

## Say this out loud

- Decentralised is a test of power: who can mint, pause, upgrade, or freeze.
- An admin key is a privileged secret. Name it. Do not treat a slogan as a substitute.
- Renounced and audited are not halos. Verified source is not a safe investment.
- RWA claims are claims to verify, not classroom proof of vaults.
- A token can live on a public chain and still be a company product.

Next: adding a token by contract, not by search.

lessons.title: Adding a token by contract, not by search
lessons.content:
# Adding a token by contract, not by search

If BscScan shows you received Crystal Stones but the wallet hides it, the wallet’s **display list** is incomplete. You add the token **as a custom token**. That is a sticker on the window. It is not a purchase. It is not an approval. It does not move coins.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to import by address and refuse every other method.

## The only beginner-safe method

1. Copy the contract from a source you already verified — for Crystal Stones:

**0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**

2. Confirm the wallet network chip is BSC (chain ID 56).
3. In the wallet, Add custom token / Import token.
4. Paste. Confirm the wallet reads symbol and decimals from the chain.
5. Do not “improve” the address from memory.

Do **not** tap a token that appeared unsolicited in the list with a “claim” button. That is Safety’s territory. Do **not** search the name and pick the highest-volume result. Do **not** import a file from Telegram. Do **not** scan a stranger’s QR.

## Why search fails, and why adding is not buying

Search returns clones ranked by who paid or who spammed. Paste beats search.

Adding a token to the display does **not** move coins and does **not** approve a spender. It is a sticker on your window. Approvals are a different popup — read the title. Module 4 will separate connect, sign, and approve. Today: if the popup says Approve, you are not adding a display sticker. You are loading a gun.

People lose this distinction under excitement. “I added Crystal Stones” is not “I bought Crystal Stones.” You can add a token you hold zero of. You can hold a token you have not added, and BscScan will still tell the truth.

The same trap exists for USDT. Importing “USDT” by name can fetch the Ethereum contract, a clone, or a spam ticker with a fake dollar column. You want the **BEP-20** USDT contract on chain 56, copied from a source you already use for that ticker — an exchange’s withdrawal help page you trust, or a bookmark you made in a calm hour — not the first search hit. If the wallet is on Ethereum when you paste a BSC contract, the import will look haunted: wrong decimals, zero that is not a real zero, or a refusal. Network chip first. Always.

A custom-token screen that asks you to **type** symbol and decimals instead of reading them from the chain is a yellow flag. Prefer the path that fetches from the contract. If you must type, you are now trusting a tweet. This academy would rather you re-copy the address than invent 18 because “everyone uses 18.”

TABLE
Method | Use? | Why
Paste known contract on BSC | Yes | Identity
Wallet name search | No | Hostile index
Telegram “import file” | No | Easy malware
Airdrop popup / Claim | No | Drain theatre
QR from a stranger | No | You cannot see the string
Send BNB to the contract to mint | No | Not a purchase; often a stuck send
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Wallet shows only BNB. BscScan token transfers show USDT and Crystal Stones.

1. The student does not open a claim site.
2. They add USDT by its **BSC** USDT contract (not Ethereum’s), after copying from a source they trust for that ticker.
3. They add Crystal Stones by 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
4. Icons appear. No claim site. No buy. No approve.
5. If a popup titled Approve appears, they reject it. That was not import.

DIAGRAM
Explorer says you hold it
        |
        v
Network chip = BSC 56
        |
        v
Custom token + paste contract
        |
        v
Display catches up

X  search by name
X  claim button
X  approve popup pretending to be import
X  “adding a token buys it”
ENDDIAGRAM

## You can finish the lab without spending

Module 6 will ask you to add BSC and a token on a practice wallet without buying. This lesson is the skill that lab uses. If you have no BNB and no tokens, you can still paste the contract and see a zero balance. Zero is a legitimate display. It is not a failure. It is not a reason to “activate” anything with a stranger.

If the wallet cannot fetch symbol and decimals, you may be on the wrong network, or the RPC is lying, or you pasted a typo. Check the chip. Re-copy. Do not type decimals from a tweet. Do not download a “token list pack” from a group. Lists are how clones arrive in bulk.

If you already see Crystal Stones in the wallet because the app recognised the contract, you do not need to import it again. Duplicate imports do not double your coins. They only confuse the window. The book did not change.

## Adding is not a listing and not a purchase

Importing a sticker does not list a token on an exchange. It does not tell Binance (example of a CEX, not the only one) anything. It does not move local currency. People post “I added it, we are listed.” They added a display row. Celebrate literacy, not a market event this classroom did not promise.

NOTE
Adding a token to the display does not move coins, does not approve a spender, and does not buy anything. This academy will not tell you to buy Crystal Stones because you now know how to import the sticker. Read the popup title. Import is not Approve.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is identity: contracts, the Crystal Stones page as literacy, clones, mechanical supply, admin power, and import-by-address. Module 4 is the human operating manual: gas, nonce, connect versus approve, replacements, and why bridges wait.

## Say this out loud

- Display lists omit tokens. Explorers do not, for that contract.
- Import by pasting the known address on chain 56. Search by name is hostile.
- Adding a token is not an approval and not a purchase.
- Claim popups are not import.
- You can add Crystal Stones as a display sticker and still hold zero. That is allowed. This course does not require a buy.

Take the quiz. Module 4: using BSC as a human being with a wallet.

lessons.title: Gas, gwei, and failed transactions
lessons.content:
# Gas, gwei, and failed transactions

**Gas** is work. **Gas price** is what you pay per unit of work, in tiny pieces of BNB. Wallets hide the maths. You still need the outcomes: a failed transaction can still cost fuel, and “failed tx is free” is a beginner myth that this lesson exists to kill.

By the end you should leave a little BNB in the tank, treat one failure as information, and refuse a site that wants a seed to “un-revert.”

## Gas is the meter, paid in the native coin

On EVM chains you bid for block space. The bid is not USDT. It is not Crystal Stones. On BSC it is **BNB**. **Gwei** is a tiny unit of that native coin, used to write the price of gas without a pile of decimal zeros. You do not need to convert gwei by hand. You need: the wallet will show a fee in BNB; that fee goes to the writer set for work, including work that failed.

If you hold a large token balance and 0 BNB, you can see the tokens and you cannot move them. Scammers will say “send gas to this address to unlock.” Real gas is taken **inside** your transaction from your own BNB, not mailed to a stranger first.

## You pay for failed work

On EVM chains, if a transaction **fails after inclusion** — out of gas, a contract said no, slippage too low — you **still pay gas** to the validators. The token transfer does not happen. Beginners see “failed” and “BNB gone” and think theft. It can be the meter running on a failed call.

That is the myth to kill: **failed tx is free.** Not on this book. Not on Ethereum. Pending-and-never-included is different: if it never lands in a block, that gas is not burned on-chain (you can replace it). Included-and-failed burns gas.

## Three common failure modes

**Out of gas.** The **gas limit** was too low for the contract’s work. Wallet estimates can be wrong on weird contracts. Raising the limit slightly is normal. Raising it to infinity on a mystery contract is how you overpay a honeypot’s loop.

**Insufficient funds for gas.** You tried to send tokens without enough BNB, or you tried to send **all** BNB including the amount needed to pay for the send. Leave a little BNB behind. Do not empty the tank to zero on a token send.

**Contract reverted.** The program said no: not enough allowance, paused token, honeypot, bad slippage, you are blacklisted. The revert message on BscScan (if any) is a clue. A “helpful” site that says “click to un-revert” is a thief.

TABLE
Wallet message | First check | Do not do
Insufficient funds | BNB balance versus gas plus value | Send BNB to a stranger to “unlock”
Failed / reverted | BscScan status and error | Retry five times on a clone dApp
Pending forever | Gas price too low, or nonce stuck | Paste a seed into an unstucker
Success but no token | Wrong token, display list, or you called something else | Claim-site “fix”
Out of gas | Limit too low for that call | Infinite limit on a mystery contract
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student tries to swap on a clone router. The transaction fails. About 0.0004 BNB is gone.

1. They think “failed is free,” so they retry. It fails again. More BNB gone.
2. They retry five times. They have paid a tutorial fee to a trap.
3. Correct: one failure → open BscScan from a bookmark → read status **failed** → stop.
4. They do not paste a seed into an “un-revert” site. They do not approve a new spender to “recover the gas.”
5. They keep remaining BNB. Small gas is why people get careless, then interact with a contract that loops.

DIAGRAM
Submit
  --> included + success --> state changed, gas paid
  --> included + fail    --> state not changed, gas still paid
  --> never included     --> no gas burned on-chain (you can replace)

Failed-and-included is not free.
Pending-forever is a nonce or fee problem, not a reason to retry blindly.
ENDDIAGRAM

## One failure is information; five retries on a clone are a donation

BSC gas is usually small. “Usually” is why people skip reading the popup. Small gas is not a reason to skip. A looping contract can still take a bite, and a drained token approval later can take the rest.

If you did not intend a swap and the **to** is a router, stop. If you intended a simple send and it reverted, read the explorer before you raise gas and smash send again. You may be on the wrong token, the wrong chain, or a paused contract.

Gwei numbers in a wallet’s advanced settings are easy to over-touch. On BSC, default estimates are usually enough for a simple send. Dragging gas to “fastest” on a 2-dollar test is how you pay more than the thing you moved. Dragging it to zero is how you sit pending and then invent nonce 13. Leave the advanced panel closed unless you are replacing a stuck nonce on purpose.

“I will pay gas in USDT” is a sentence from a different product, or from a liar. On this book, writers take BNB. A dApp that offers to “take the fee in token” is wrapping extra contract risk around the meter. Basic does not need that wrapper. Keep a little BNB and use it as the meter.

NOTE
Academy rule: failed transactions can still cost BNB. Leave fuel in the tank. One failure is information. Five retries on a clone is a donation. Nobody needs your seed to “refund gas.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The meter is now honest. Next: nonce — the send counter that, when stuck, makes people think BSC is down.

## Say this out loud

- Gas on BSC is paid in BNB. Tokens do not pay the meter.
- A transaction that fails after inclusion can still cost BNB. Failed is not free.
- Leave BNB for gas. Do not empty the tank to zero on a token send, and do not mail gas to a stranger to “unlock.”
- Out of gas, insufficient funds, and revert are different problems. Read the explorer once before retrying.
- One failure is information. Five retries on a clone dApp is a donation.

Next: nonce, pending, and the stuck send.

lessons.title: Nonce, pending, and stuck sends
lessons.content:
# Nonce, pending, and stuck sends

Every EVM account has a **nonce**: how many transactions it has already had included. The next transaction must use the next number. This stops replay and orders your sends.

By the end of this lesson you should wait or replace the stuck number, and you should refuse to pile new sends — or paste a seed into an “unstucker.”

## Nonce is your send counter, not a mystery tax

If your last successful transaction used nonce 11, the next one must be 12. If 12 is pending with too-low gas, nonce 13 (your “retry”) sits behind it **forever**. Wallets sometimes hide this and you think BSC is down.

Pending means broadcast, not included — Module 1. A stuck pending nonce is a traffic jam you caused by bidding too low, or by losing connectivity, or by replacing badly. It is not a reason to create a new wallet and hand funds to a helper.

Nonce is not a fee. It is not a password. It is not “the RPC PIN.” You will not find it on a seed phrase card. Explorers show it on a transaction page as a number. Your next send is last-success plus one. If a site asks you to paste a seed to “reset nonce,” they are stealing. If a site asks you to send leftover funds to a recovery address to “clear the counter,” they are stealing with extra steps. The counter lives on the book. It increments when a transaction from your address is included. That is all.

Wallets sometimes show “already known” or “replacement transaction underpriced.” Those sentences mean: you tried to reuse a nonce without bidding enough to beat the one already sitting in the waiting room. Raise the bid on **that** number, or wait. Do not invent nonce 99 because a forum said so.

## What to do, as a beginner

1. Look at BscScan address page: pending versus last **successful** nonce.
2. Do not fire five new sends.
3. In MetaMask (example of a wallet app), “speed up” or “cancel” the **stuck** nonce. Cancel is a 0-value transaction to yourself with the same nonce and higher gas. Trust Wallet UIs differ; the idea is the same: replace the stuck nonce, do not stack new ones.
4. If you do not understand the UI, wait. Cheap gas on BSC often clears. Waiting is underrated.

The next lesson is the full picture of speed-up and cancel, and why refreshing the app is not a chain action. Today you need the queue: one stuck number blocks the next numbers.

## What not to do

- a “nonce unstucker” website that wants a seed
- switching RPC ten times and sending more
- creating a new wallet and transferring **via a helper** who will hold the funds
- treating a stuck 8-minute BSC transaction as an emergency that justifies a new APK

Hardware wallets and some mobile apps make replacement awkward. Then waiting is the professional move.

TABLE
Picture | Action | Trap
One pending, nothing after | Wait or speed up that nonce | Unstucker site
Many pendings | You queued behind a stuck nonce; stop adding | “Just keep sending”
Success on explorer, wallet pending | RPC lag; refresh the view, do not resend | Duplicate payment
Wallet says failed, explorer pending | Believe the explorer | Smash send
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Nonce 12 is pending 20 minutes. A student sends again (nonce 13). Both sit.

1. They open a “fast BSC” dApp, sign something unrelated, still pending.
2. An hour later nonce 12 lands, then 13 — a duplicate USDT send they did not want. They paid twice.
3. Correct was: wait or replace nonce 12 only.
4. They look at BscScan. They see two pending. They stop.
5. They do not paste a seed. They either wait or use the wallet’s speed-up on nonce 12.

DIAGRAM
Nonce 11 success
Nonce 12 pending  <--- only this may be replaced
Nonce 13 queued behind 12
Nonce 14 would queue behind 13

Do not add 14.
Replace 12, or wait.
ENDDIAGRAM

## The explorer is the referee, not the app banner

If BscScan shows success and the wallet still shows pending, the book is ahead of the window. Wait, pull to refresh, or switch RPC once if you know a documented one. Do not send again. Duplicate sends are how a “stuck” moment becomes a double payment.

If BscScan shows nothing and the wallet says sent, the RPC may have accepted a message the validators are ignoring. Still: one nonce. Wait or replace. Do not invent a second instruction.

Nonce gaps are rare for beginners and usually mean a wallet bug or a replacement that landed in an order you did not expect. Do not fill a gap because a forum said to “post empty transactions for missing numbers.” Look at the last **successful** nonce on the explorer. The next one is plus one. That is the whole arithmetic.

If you used two devices with the same seed at once, they can fight over the same counter. One phone broadcasts 12, the other also broadcasts 12 with a different job. One wins. The other dies or sits. For practice, one device. The wallets course already preferred that. BSC does not cancel the advice.

NOTE
A stuck 8-minute BSC transaction is not an emergency that justifies a new app or a seed-paste. Unstucker sites are hostile. Nonce is a counter. Treat it as a counter.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can see the queue. Next: the three popups that are not the same — connect, sign, approve — because “I only connected” is how USDT leaves later.

## Say this out loud

- Nonce is your send counter. The next transaction must use the next number.
- A stuck pending nonce blocks every later number. Do not pile new sends.
- Wait or replace the stuck nonce. Do not paste a seed into an unstucker.
- If the explorer shows success and the wallet shows pending, that is lag, not a reason to resend.
- Cheap BSC gas often clears if you wait. Waiting is a skill.

Next: Connect versus sign versus approve.

lessons.title: Connect versus sign versus approve
lessons.content:
# Connect versus sign versus approve

Three different popups. Mixing them is how “I only connected” becomes “my USDT left.” This is the BSC-flavoured version of a lesson Safety will repeat until it is a reflex.

By the end you should read the title of every popup, reject what you cannot explain, and know that viewing BscScan needs no approve.

## Connect: the site learns your address

**Connect** means the site learns **which address** you selected. It cannot take coins by connect alone. It can now **show you** tailored scams (“your address is eligible”). Connecting to a random site is still unwise because of that targeting, but it is not a transfer.

Connect is not KYC. Connect is not a purchase. Connect is not an approval. It is a handshake that reveals a public 0x. Public is the word: that address was already on a public book. Revealing it to a hostile site still gives them a targeting list with you on it.

## Sign: a message, sometimes a delayed yes

A **signature** proves you control the key. Some messages are logins. Some are **typed data** that a scam will later use as a **permit** (a gasless-style approval). Read: does this look like “Sign in to this site” or “Permit unlimited USDT”? If you cannot tell, **reject**.

Signing is not “free so it must be harmless.” The harm is not the gas. The harm is what you attested. If a site needs a signature to “prove you are human” and the text is a blob, reject. You can use BscScan without this.

## Approve: you load a spender’s gun

**Approve** is an on-chain transaction. You pay gas in BNB. You tell a token contract: “this **spender** may move up to N of my tokens.” DEX routers need some allowance if you ever swap on purpose. **Unlimited** allowance to a mystery spender is how drainers finish you days later without another click that looks like a send.

Approve is not a send. Tokens may not move yet. The next **transferFrom** can move them without a popup that says “send.” BscScan will show the approval, then later a transfer from your address **by the spender**. The chain is honest. The reading was not.

Beginners do not need to approve anything to **view** a token on BscScan. Pancake-style sites will ask for approve. Fake Crystal Stones dashboards will too. The difference is **which spender** and **why you are there**. If you are there because a sponsored link said “dashboard,” you are in the wrong shop.

TABLE
Popup | Moves tokens now? | Danger | Beginner default
Connect | No | Targeting, fake UI after | Only to sites you typed yourself
Sign message | Not by itself; permits can be a delayed yes | Read or reject | Reject blobs
Send / transfer | Yes | Wrong address / network | Tiny test, explorer
Approve | Not yet — it loads the gun | Unlimited + unknown spender | Reject if you cannot name the spender
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student connects to a “Crystal Stones dashboard” from a sponsored link.

1. Connect succeeds. They think they are safe because nothing moved.
2. Next popup: Approve USDT unlimited. They think it is KYC. They confirm.
3. Later a transferFrom empties USDT. BscScan shows: first an approval, then a transfer from their address by the spender.
4. The chain did what they signed. A helper now offers to “reverse the approve” via another site. That helper is the second drain.
5. Correct: connect was already optional. Approve was the loaded gun. Viewing BscScan needed neither.

DIAGRAM
Connect --> site knows your address          (not a payment)
Sign    --> you attested a message           (read it; permits exist)
Approve --> spender may take tokens later    (loads the gun)
Send    --> tokens move now

Viewing BscScan sits in none of these boxes.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Read the title, then the spender, then the amount

Ritual:

- Title says Connect? You are revealing an address.
- Title says Sign / Sign in? Read the message. Blob? Reject.
- Title says Approve / Set allowance? Name the spender. Unlimited? That is a loud yes. Mystery spender? Reject.
- Title says Send / Confirm transaction with a transfer? Check network chip, token, amount, destination.

If you cannot name those objects, you are not ready to press. That is not cowardice. That is Basic.

Permit-style signatures deserve one extra sentence because they blur Sign and Approve. A **permit** is a signed message that a contract can later use as if you had approved, sometimes without a separate approve transaction. You may not see a BNB fee at the moment you sign. You may still have loaded the gun. If the message lists a spender and a token and a huge amount, it is not a login. Reject. Safety will show more of this family. Today: blob plus token plus spender equals no.

You do not need to connect a wallet to BscScan to finish this course’s labs. If a page will not show a public balance without connect, you are on the wrong page.

NOTE
The Safety course repeats this until it is a reflex. Here you only need the BSC-flavoured version: real DEX use will ask for approve; fake dashboards will too. Beginners do not need to approve anything to view a token on BscScan. This academy will never ask you to approve a spender in a DM.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Three popups now have names. Next: speeding up, cancelling, and why “refresh the app” is not a chain action — the sibling of the nonce lesson, with the myth that pulling down on a screen unsticks a book.

## Say this out loud

- Connect reveals the selected address. It is not a transfer.
- Sign can still be a permit. Read or reject. A blob is a no.
- Approve loads a spender’s gun. Unlimited plus unknown spender is how drainers finish you later.
- Viewing the real BscScan needs no connect, no sign, no approve.
- “I only connected” is not a defence if you also approved.

Next: speeding up, cancelling, and why refreshing the app is not a chain action.

lessons.title: Speeding up, cancelling, and why refresh is not a chain action
lessons.content:
# Speeding up, cancelling, and why refresh is not a chain action

Wallets offer buttons that look like magic: Speed up, Cancel, Refresh. Only two of those talk to the book, and they talk by **replacing a nonce**. Pulling down on a screen does not unstick a blockchain.

By the end of this lesson you should know what speed-up and cancel actually broadcast, and you should stop treating the app as the chain.

## Speed up is the same nonce with a higher bid

**Speed up** means: take the stuck instruction (same nonce, same intent) and rebroadcast it with a higher gas price so writers prefer it. If it works, one of the two versions lands. The nonce is consumed once. You pay more BNB for the same job.

You are not “pushing the chain.” You are raising your bid for the same queue slot. If the original was a USDT send to Sam, the replacement should still be a USDT send to Sam, not a new adventure.

## Cancel is a 0-value send to yourself with the same nonce

**Cancel**, in MetaMask-style wallets (example, not endorsement), usually means: broadcast a tiny (often 0) native send **to your own address**, same nonce, higher gas. If that replacement lands first, the original instruction dies. You paid gas to do nothing, on purpose, to free the queue.

Cancel does not rewind a transaction that already succeeded. If BscScan already says success, there is nothing to cancel. You would be trying to spend a nonce that is already used. The wallet may confuse you. The explorer should not.

Trust Wallet and other mobile UIs may not expose these buttons cleanly. Then waiting is the professional move, as the nonce lesson said. A stuck few minutes on BSC is common. A helper who needs a seed to cancel is a thief.

## Refresh is a window action, not a book action

**Refresh** reloads what the RPC last told the app. It can clear a stuck spinner. It can fetch a success the app missed. It cannot:

- include a pending transaction
- raise gas
- cancel a nonce
- reverse a send
- “unstick” validators
- turn testnet coins into local currency

If the book has not included you, pulling down on the screen is like staring at a post-office window. Useful to see. Not a stamp.

People mash refresh, then mash send. That is how nonce 12 and 13 both exist. Believe the explorer, then wait or replace.

TABLE
Button or habit | Talks to the chain? | What it actually does
Speed up | Yes, if it broadcasts a replacement | Same nonce, higher gas, same intent
Cancel | Yes, if it broadcasts a 0-value self-send | Same nonce, higher gas, original dies if this lands
Refresh / pull down | No | Reloads the window from an RPC
Force-close the app | No | Restarts the window
Reinstall the app | No | Still the same book if you still have the key
New APK from a helper | Hostile | Often a drain
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Kemi’s USDT send sits pending. She force-closes Trust Wallet, reopens it, pulls to refresh, and the banner still says pending.

1. She almost sends again. She remembers nonce.
2. She opens BscScan from a bookmark. The hash is pending. The book agrees with the banner, for once.
3. Refresh did nothing to the book. That is correct behaviour. Refresh is not supposed to stamp a page.
4. She waits. On BSC, cheap gas often clears. Ten minutes later the explorer says success.
5. If it had sat an hour, she could try the wallet’s speed-up on **that** nonce, or wait more. She does not download a “BSC booster” APK.

DIAGRAM
Stuck pending
   |
   +--> Refresh app     --> new picture of the same book (no new page)
   +--> Speed up        --> replacement, same nonce, higher bid
   +--> Cancel          --> 0-value to self, same nonce, higher bid
   +--> Send again      --> new nonce, queued behind the stuck one (bad)
   +--> Helper APK      --> drain

The book moves when a writer includes a transaction.
The app moving is not the book moving.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Explorer first, button second

Before speed-up or cancel:

- Paste the hash on BscScan.
- If success, stop. Refresh the wallet. Do not replace.
- If failed-and-included, the nonce is already consumed. You may send a **new** transaction if you still want the job. That is not a cancel.
- If pending, you may wait, speed up, or cancel.
- If the hash never appeared, the RPC may have eaten a ghost. Wait; do not spray new nonces.

Speed-up that changes the destination is not speed-up. It is a new idea wearing an old nonce. Some malware wallets offer “speed up” that actually builds a send to a thief. Watch the **to** and the token row on the replacement, the same way you watch the first send. If cancel is not a self-send, it is not cancel.

On BSC, “stuck” often means “two minutes feels like a year because we were told the chain is instant.” Instant is a marketing word. Fast is real. Pending is still pending. Set a timer. Look at the explorer once. Then look again. Do not look every two seconds in a group chat that is offering APKs.

NOTE
Refreshing the app is not a chain action. Speed-up and cancel are nonce replacements. If you do not see those buttons, waiting is allowed. Nobody needs your seed to refresh a public book.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The app is a window; replacements are extra bids; refresh is not a stamp. Last lesson of this module: bridges, in one honest stretch of prose, because they are how people lose funds and Basic does not use them yet.

## Say this out loud

- Speed up is the same nonce with a higher gas bid, not a prayer.
- Cancel is usually a 0-value transaction to yourself with the same nonce and higher gas.
- Refresh reloads the window. It does not include, cancel, or reverse a transaction.
- If the explorer already says success, there is nothing to cancel and nothing to resend.
- A booster APK or unstucker site is hostile.

Next: bridges in one honest lesson — Basic does not use them yet; they are how people lose funds.

lessons.title: Bridges in one honest paragraph
lessons.content:
# Bridges in one honest paragraph

A **bridge** tries to represent value on a second book, usually by locking coins on one chain and minting a representation on the other. That extra machine is extra trust. Bridges are a major hack magnet. This Basic course does not use them. They are how people lose funds.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to refuse a bridge URL, stay on one book, and say why “we are multi-chain” is not a beginner instruction.

## The honest paragraph, then the unpacking

Here is the paragraph, stated as policy: **do not bridge practice funds because a group dropped a URL.** You already have enough ways to lose money on one chain — wrong network, no gas, fake token, unlimited approve. A bridge adds a second book, a lock contract, a mint contract, and often a website that can lie about all three. Stay on BNB Smart Chain for this track. If you need USDT on BSC, withdraw BEP-20 USDT from a venue onto chain 56. Do not “wrap,” “teleport,” or “migrate” through a caption.

That is the lesson. The rest is why the paragraph is not cowardice.

## What a bridge actually is

Two books do not share balances. Module 2 already said this. A bridge is a machine in the middle:

- you send asset A on chain 1 to a contract or custodian
- something mints or releases asset B on chain 2
- you now hold a representation, not necessarily “the same coins teleported”

If the lock is hacked, the representation on the other side can become an unbacked IOU. If the website is fake, you approved a drainer and never reached a real lock. If the representation is a clone token with a similar name, you bridged into a honeypot.

Official-looking bridges still get hacked. Random bridges in chats are theft with extra steps. This classroom will not give you a “safe bridge list” for Basic, because the skill you need first is **not bridging**.

## Why beginners lose funds here

The pitch is always convenience: “BSC is cheap, Ethereum is where the real one lives, just bridge.” Or: “Crystal Stones is multi-chain now, bridge to claim.” Or: “Your USDT is stuck on the wrong network, bridge it back.”

Each pitch skips the objects:

- which lock contract
- which minted representation (address, not sticker)
- who runs the operators
- what happens if the website dies mid-way
- what gas you need on **both** books to finish

People also bridge because they already mixed ERC-20 and BEP-20 and want a miracle. Sometimes a venue’s own withdrawal on the correct network is the boring fix. Sometimes you open the other book with that book’s gas. A chat-group bridge is the expensive fix.

TABLE
Situation | Boring fix | Bridge pitch
Need USDT on BSC | Withdraw BEP-20 USDT, chain 56 | “Bridge from Ethereum, sponsored URL”
Sent ERC-20 to your 0x | Open Ethereum, need ETH for gas | “Bridge to BSC to see it in Trust Wallet”
Clone says multi-chain | Ignore; verify the BSC contract | “Bridge to the new Crystal Stones”
Stuck pending on BSC | Wait or replace nonce | “Bridge out to unstick”
Want cheaper fees | You are already on BSC | “Bridge to a mystery L2”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A WhatsApp status offers “official Crystal Stones bridge — migrate to the new chain this weekend or lose your tokens.”

1. Funke does not click. Academy staff do not migrate people in statuses.
2. She opens the long-standing project site, not the status.
3. She verifies 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on BscScan. The object this academy means is still on chain 56.
4. She does not connect a wallet to the bridge site. She does not approve a spender named Router or Migrator.
5. She stays on one book. She still has not been told to buy. She has been told not to teleport.

DIAGRAM
Book A  -- lock / custodian / website --  Book B
              |                |
              v                v
           hack target     minted lookalike

Basic track: stay on BSC (chain 56).
Do not follow a URL into the middle box.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What to do instead, for this academy

Stay on BNB Smart Chain. One explorer: BscScan. One gas coin: BNB. One token standard: BEP-20. One Crystal Stones contract to verify. If paid tracks open, tuition rails are USDT on BEP-20, not “USDT somewhere” and not a bridge of Crystal Stones token.

Intermediate will do contracts and DeFi for real, including the right to learn why bridges are hard. Advanced is not “how to chase every chain.” Basic’s job is to keep you on one book long enough to read it.

If you already bridged by accident before this lesson, do not “bridge back” through the same chat. Open the destination book’s explorer. See what representation you hold. Safety’s incident habits apply. This course’s rule going forward is still: stay on 56 for practice.

NOTE
Academy rule: Basic does not use bridges. They are how people lose funds. “Multi-chain” in a caption is not a homework assignment. Official-looking lock contracts still get hacked; chat-group bridges are assumed hostile. Stay on chain 56 for this track.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is the operating manual: the meter, the queue, the three popups, the replacement buttons, and a closed door labelled Bridge. Module 5 makes BscScan boring so you do not need a helper to read your own book.

## Say this out loud

- A bridge locks on one book and mints a representation on another. Extra machine, extra trust, extra hacks.
- Basic does not use bridges. Stay on BNB Smart Chain, chain ID 56.
- Wrong-network USDT is often fixed by opening the correct book or withdrawing correctly, not by a chat URL.
- Surprise “migrate this weekend” bridges are clone theatre.
- This academy will not tell you to teleport Crystal Stones, USDT, or BNB because a caption said multi-chain.

Take the quiz. Module 5: BscScan until it is boring.
