lessons.title: The address page
lessons.content:
# The address page

Paste an 0x into BscScan. You get a **dossier**. Not a social profile. Not a credit score. A public list of what this book says about that address: native balance, token rows, signed instructions, token transfers, internal hops.

By the end of this lesson you should pick the panel that matches the question, hide spam tokens with fake USD values, and bookmark the real explorer instead of walking in through a chat link.

## Domain, then paste, then pick a panel

Use a bookmark for **bscscan.com**. Visiting your own address through a chat link is how fake explorers get a session. If the page demands Connect Wallet to show a public number, you left the real product.

An address page is for **one** 0x. Your wallet address is an EOA. A token contract is a different page with extra token tabs. Do not mix them. If you paste the Crystal Stones contract, you are reading the program, not your pocket. If you paste your receive address, you are reading your pocket.

## BNB balance is the fuel gauge

Native BNB sits at the top. If this is 0, token sends will fail for gas even if tokens are huge. That is Module 2 and Module 4 again. The address page is where you confirm it without trusting the app’s spinner.

A huge BNB number you do not remember earning is either a different address, a screenshot lie, or a unit you misread. Believe the explorer after you confirmed the domain and the 0x.

## BEP-20 tokens, including poison

A list of token contracts that have a balance for this address. Hide zero spam if the UI allows. **Poison tokens** with huge fake USD values appear here — dust with a made-up price so you look rich, or so you click a “claim” or “convert” link. Do not click those links. Do not swap the spam “to recover the value.” Do not approve a spender to “clean” the list.

The USD column on a mystery ticker is theatre. The Crystal Stones row, if present, should match the contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 if that is the object you mean. Name first, then amount.

## Transaction list versus token transfers

**Transactions** are what this key signed (and some it received as native). Useful for “what did I approve?” and “what did I send as BNB?”

**Token transfers (BEP-20)** is the view you want for USDT or Crystal Stones incoming. If you are checking whether you were paid 100 Crystal Stones, this is the panel. Filter the contract. Read from, to, amount, status.

**Internal txs** are BNB moved by **contracts** on this address’s behalf — a DEX sending leftover BNB back, for example. Beginners skip this and then think a swap “stole” BNB that was actually a hop. The next two lessons unpack hops. Today: know the panel exists so you do not panic at extra rows.

TABLE
Panel | Question it answers | Trap
BNB balance | Can they pay gas? | Treating 0 as “the wallet is broken”
BEP-20 | What tokens does the book say they hold? | Fake USD on spam tokens; claim links
Tx list | What did this key sign? | Missing a token receive that lives on another tab
Token transfers | Did a specific ticker move? | Looking at a clone ticker with a similar name
Internal | Did a contract move native BNB in a hop? | Calling every hop theft
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** You are checking whether you were paid 100 Crystal Stones.

1. Bookmark bscscan.com. Paste **your** address, not a screenshot of someone else’s.
2. Ignore the spam token with a $50,000 sticker. Do not click it.
3. Open Token transfers. Filter the Crystal Stones contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
4. If there is a row from the payer, amount 100, success, you were paid. If there is only a fake token named similarly, you were not.
5. You still do not connect a wallet from an ad banner.

DIAGRAM
Address page (real bscscan.com)
  BNB balance     --> fuel
  BEP-20 list     --> rows, including spam (do not click)
  Signed txs      --> what this key authorised
  Token transfers --> ticker payments
  Internals       --> native hops inside programs

Pick the panel that matches the question.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Bookmark your own address on the real explorer

Once. From a domain you typed. Then use that bookmark when a stranger says “check this.” You can still paste a hash they send — hashes are public — but you paste it into **your** explorer, not theirs.

The address page also shows **analytics** and ads. Treat analytics as optional decoration. Treat ads as hostile until you have a reason not to. A banner that says your address is “flagged” and must connect to unflag is not BscScan’s core product. Public pages do not parent you with a connect button.

If you paste a contract address by mistake, you will see a contract dossier, not your pocket. The BNB on a token contract is not “your” BNB. Module 2 already warned you not to mail fuel into a program. The address page will tempt you to click **Write**. Do not. You are here to read.

NOTE
Bookmark your own address on **real** BscScan. Visiting it through a chat link is how fake explorers get a session. Fake USD values on spam tokens are bait. Public pages do not need your seed.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The dossier now has named drawers. Next: the transaction page, field by field, so a hash is something you can read aloud.

## Say this out loud

- An address page is a dossier for one 0x on this book, not a social profile.
- Token transfers settle ticker arguments. The native tx list is a different drawer.
- Fake USD values on mystery tokens are bait. Do not click claim links.
- Zero BNB on the address page means you cannot move tokens, even if the token list looks rich.
- Bookmark the real explorer. Do not walk in through a chat link.

Next: the transaction page, field by field.

lessons.title: The transaction page
lessons.content:
# The transaction page

A **tx hash** is the id of one instruction. Paste it on BscScan. You get a page that should answer: did it land, who signed, who was called, what native BNB moved, what tokens moved, what it cost.

By the end of this lesson you should read those fields in order, and you should share hashes — not seeds — when you ask a knowledgeable friend.

## Status is the first word, not the last

**Success**, **fail**, **pending**. Fail still has a hash. Success is not “success for the token you wanted” until you read token transfers. A successful call to the wrong contract is a successful mistake.

Pending is Module 1: not paid. Failed-and-included is Module 4: gas may still be gone. Do not let a green UI in a wallet outrun a red status on the explorer, or the reverse. The explorer is the referee if the domain is real.

## From, to, and value

**From** is the key that signed, for a normal send. **To** may be a person or a contract. Click through. If you intended a friend and **to** is a router, you signed a swap or a drain, not a gift.

**Value** is native BNB. Token sends: often 0. You already know this. Still look. If you intended to send BNB and value is 0, you may have signed a token call instead. If you intended USDT and value is a lot of BNB, you may have signed the wrong thing.

## Token transfers and the fee

**Transaction action / tokens transferred** is the human summary. Still verify amount and **token address**, not only the sticker. Crystal Stones must be 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 if that is the object you mean. A sticker “CST” on a different contract is a different object.

**Gas used / price / BNB fee** is what the send cost. Useful when arguing “the exchange took 8 USDT” — sometimes it was a different transaction’s fee, sometimes it was the CEX withdrawal fee, sometimes it was a failed loop. Name the hash, then the fee.

**Logs / input data** exist. Later-you may care. Today: know they exist. Do not paste input data into a “decoder” you just met if it asks to connect a wallet. The next lesson but one will show approve as something you can see without decoding hex by hand.

TABLE
Field | Beginner read | Common misread
Status | Did it land? | Green wallet banner versus explorer
To | Person or contract? | Assuming to is always the friend on a token send
Value | Native BNB only | “0 means failed”
Token transfers | The actual USDT / Crystal Stones movement | Believing the sticker without the contract
Fee | BNB spent | Blaming a CEX for an on-chain fee, or the reverse
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Hash from an exchange withdrawal.

1. From: a venue hot wallet. To: your EOA.
2. Token transferred: USDT on the BSC contract you expected, amount 49 after a 1 USDT fee they already showed.
3. Status success. Native value 0, which is normal.
4. Argument over. Wallet still catching up is irrelevant. Refresh is a window. The book already wrote the page.
5. You share this hash with a friend who asked “did it leave?” You do not share a seed.

DIAGRAM
Hash --> status --> from/to --> token transfers (contract + amount) --> fee
If those are right, the tx did the job.
If to is a mystery contract and you meant a friend, the job was not a gift.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Hashes are public; seeds are not

A hash cannot drain you. Anyone can look it up. That is the point of a public book. A seed can drain you. When you ask for help, paste the hash and the address — the public ones — into a conversation with someone you actually know. Not into a “support” form that also asks for words.

If a helper says they cannot help without the seed, they cannot help. They can steal.

Write a four-line card when you are checking a payment, and keep it until the argument is over:

- Hash: (paste)
- Status: success / fail / pending
- Token contract + amount + recipient (or native BNB value + recipient)
- Fee in BNB

That card is what a shopkeeper reads. It is also what you send to a knowledgeable friend. It is not a screenshot. It is not “the wallet went green.” If the card’s token contract is not the one you named, the payment you named did not happen, even if status is success.

Some explorers show a friendly **Transaction Action** summary (“Transfer 20 USDT to …”). Use it as a hint, then still click the token address. Summaries can sticker-match a clone. The contract string cannot, if you compare it.

Input data that looks like a hex dump is not a second payment. Do not paste it into a “decoder bot.” If you needed a human method name, BscScan’s Method field is the beginner tool. Module 5’s logs lesson will continue that. Today: status, from, to, value, token tab, fee.

NOTE
Share hashes, not seeds, when you ask a knowledgeable friend. A hash cannot drain you. A seed can. Success on the explorer is not success for the ticker you wanted until the token-transfer row matches the contract you named.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

A hash is now a document you can narrate. Next: three different records people smash together — internal transfers, token transfers, and BNB value.

## Say this out loud

- Paste the hash on the real explorer. Status first: pending, fail, or success.
- To-a-contract means you called a program. To-a-friend should look like that if you meant a gift of BNB.
- Value 0 is normal for token sends. Look at token transfers for the ticker and the contract.
- The BNB fee is on this page. Name it before you blame a venue or a “hidden tax.”
- Hashes are public. Seeds are not. Anyone who needs a seed to read a hash is a thief.

Next: internal transfers versus token transfers versus BNB value.

lessons.title: Internal transfers versus token transfers versus BNB value
lessons.content:
# Internal transfers versus token transfers versus BNB value

Three different records. Mixing them is how people misread swaps, panic-post in a group, and then sign a “revoke” on a helper’s site that is the actual drain.

By the end of this lesson you should check **final balances versus intent**, and you should treat a helper who needs a new signature to “explain a hop” as hostile.

## BNB value is the native line

The transaction’s **value** field is native BNB attached to that instruction. Simple send of BNB to a friend: this line is the story. Token send: this line is often 0. Swap selling BNB: this line may be the BNB you spent into the router.

If you look only here, you will think USDT failed, or you will miss that you just dumped BNB into a program.

## Token transfers are the BEP-20 story

The token contract emitted “A sent N to B.” This is your USDT / Crystal Stones story. Filter by contract address, not by ticker sticker. A swap may show several token rows: you gave token A, you received token B, a pool address sat in the middle.

If you wanted to send USDT to a friend, success looks like one token transfer, your EOA → friend EOA, on the USDT contract you meant. If you see a router in the middle and you did not intend a swap, you signed the wrong app.

## Internal transactions are native hops inside programs

A contract called another contract and moved **native BNB**. A DEX router might: take your BNB, send BNB to a pool, send leftover BNB back. You will see internals that are **not** you signing each hop. Your **one** signature authorised the whole bundle.

Why it looks like theft: you signed one swap. BscScan shows four internals and three token hops. A scammer zooms in on one hop — “they took your BNB to this pool.” That is how the swap works. The question is whether the **final** balances match what the UI promised, not whether hops exist.

If you did **not** intend a swap and you still see a router as **to**, that is a different story — you signed the wrong app. Then we care a lot about hops.

BNB value, token transfers, and internals can all be true at once on one hash. A swap selling BNB for USDT might show: native value into the router, token transfers of USDT out to you, internals of BNB hopping through a pair. None of those rows is “the extra secret theft row.” They are the same job, sliced three ways. Theft, when it is theft, looks like: you meant a friend, **to** is a mystery spender, token transfers leave to an address you do not know, and a helper wants a new signature. Different picture.

If you are only sending BNB to a person, you should not need a token tab to explain it, and you should not need internals. If those extra rows appear, you called a program. Stop and name the program before you add a second hash.

A third misread: BNB **value** is 1.2, internals show 1.2 leaving to a router, token tab shows USDT in. Someone says “they took your 1.2 twice.” They counted the same native coins in two drawers. Count each drawer once. End balances still win.

TABLE
You wanted | Success looks like | Panic misread
Send USDT to a friend | One token transfer, your EOA → friend EOA | “Value 0 so it failed”
Send BNB to a friend | Native value, no token needed | “Internal row means a hack”
Swap BNB → USDT on a DEX you meant | Multiple hops; you end with more USDT, less BNB | “The pool stole BNB”
Approve only | Approval event, tokens not moved yet | “Nothing happened so I should retry”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student swaps a little BNB for USDT on a real DEX they meant to use.

1. They see a hop to a pair contract. They panic-post in a group.
2. A “helper” says it is a drain, please sign a revoke via **their** site.
3. The helper’s site is the drain. Final balances already matched the swap.
4. The student needed a reading lesson, not a helper. They check ending BNB down, USDT up, fees in BNB, status success.
5. They do not sign the helper’s revoke. They bookmark BscScan harder.

DIAGRAM
One signature
    --> router
          --> pool
          --> token contract
          --> maybe BNB refund

Many rows, one intent.
Check end balances versus what you meant.
If you did not mean a swap, a router as to is a problem.
ENDDIAGRAM

## End balances are the adult summary

Write four numbers when you are confused:

- BNB before and after (fuel plus any native you meant to move)
- token A before and after
- token B before and after
- fee on the hash

If those four match the job, hops are plumbing. If they do not, you have a real problem — wrong app, failed swap, clone token — and Safety’s incident habits matter more than a group helper.

NOTE
If you did not intend a swap and you still see a router as to, that is not plumbing to ignore. Then hops matter. A helper who needs a signature to explain a hop is selling a drain. Token tab = BEP-20 story. Internals = native hops. Value = native BNB on that instruction.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Three records, one intent, end balances as the summary. Next: the token tracker and holders — and why a big holder is not a promise.

## Say this out loud

- Native value is BNB on that transaction. Token sends often show 0 there.
- Token transfers are the BEP-20 story. Filter by contract, not by sticker.
- Internal transactions are often normal contract hops. Check final balances versus intent.
- A helper who needs a new signature to “explain” a hop is selling a drain.
- If you did not intend a swap, a router as to is not a hop to shrug at.

Next: token tracker, holders, and why a big holder is not a promise.

lessons.title: Token tracker, holders, and why a big holder is not a promise
lessons.content:
# Token tracker, holders, and why a big holder is not a promise

BscScan’s **token tracker** is the token’s homepage on the explorer: supply, holders, transfers, contract. You met it in Module 3. This lesson slows down on **holders**, because screenshots of “whales” are used to sell courage and to sell panic.

By the end you should read concentration as a fact, not as a prophecy, and you should not harass holders in DMs.

## The tracker is identity plus statistics

Paste 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. You should see a token tracker for that contract on the real domain. Circulating and total supply figures here are contract-side (and sometimes explorer-side estimates). They are still not market cap as a promise. They are not local currency. They are not a vault.

Transfers, you already use. Holders, you will now use without turning it into a hunt.

## Who a “big holder” might be

A large balance can be:

- a **liquidity pool** contract (tokens sitting in a pair so people can swap)
- a **centralised exchange** hot or cold wallet (an IOU factory, not a fan)
- a **treasury** or team wallet (power, not a halo)
- a **locker** contract (maybe locked, maybe not — Intermediate)
- a person
- a clone’s marketing wallet on a different contract you opened by mistake

You often cannot tell from the 0x alone. Labels on BscScan help when they exist and can be wrong when they are crowdsourced. “Whale bought” in a group is usually a hop into a venue or a pool, or a lie.

A big holder is **not**:

- a promise the price will rise
- proof a mineral vault is full
- a reason to copy-trade their next move
- a person you should DM to beg for tokens
- a reason this academy tells you to buy

## Concentration is a layer of the decentralisation test

Foundations: if ten wallets own almost everything, those ten people *are* the economy, even if the software looks open. That is **holder concentration**. It is a different question from “how many validators exist” and from “is the source verified.”

You can look. You should not turn looking into a conspiracy hobby on day one. You should not publish someone’s address with a threat. You should not assume an exchange wallet is “the team dumping” every time it sends to a pool.

Holders also change when people deposit to a CEX: many small addresses become one hot wallet. That looks like “a whale accumulated” if you only watch the CEX address, and like “retail dumped” if you only watch the small ones. Both captions can be written from the same hour of transfers. The tracker does not know the story. It knows balances.

If you are using Crystal Stones as the case, remember the RWA layer again. A large treasury-looking wallet does not prove gold, lithium, or a title deed. It proves that 0x holds a number in the contract 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Numbers on a list are not vaults. This classroom will not pretend they are.

TABLE
Thing you see | Adult reading | Not a license for
Top holder is a pool | Normal if people trade the token | “Guaranteed liquidity forever”
Top holder is a CEX | Many users’ IOUs behind one address | “The exchange promised listing forever”
Top holder is an unlabeled EOA | Power is concentrated | Doxxing, begging, copy-trading
Many tiny holders | Distribution exists | “Community will never sell”
A screenshot of holders | Easy to fake (next lesson) | Belief without the live page
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A Telegram caption: “whale just bought 8 million Crystal Stones — listing imminent.”

1. Emeka does not buy. This academy did not tell him to.
2. He opens the tracker from a bookmark, contract pasted, real domain.
3. He opens the large incoming transfer. The “whale” is a pool or a venue wallet, or it is a transfer between two team-looking addresses, or it is real. He may not know.
4. He notices the caption skipped the contract address. A clone tracker would have served the same caption.
5. He closes the tab. A big holder is not a promise. He has homework in Safety next, not a long position from a classroom.

DIAGRAM
Token tracker
   supply   --> contract number, not a vault
   transfers --> payments
   holders  --> concentration
                 |
                 +--> pool / CEX / treasury / person / unknown
                 |
                 v
            a fact about the list, not a prophecy
ENDDIAGRAM

## Do not harass holders

Public book does not mean public consent to be bothered. Do not DM random large addresses. Do not scrape the list for “leads.” Do not treat a holder as customer support. If you need the project, use official channels you already verified — and still do not send a seed.

RWA claims stay in their layer. A large holder does not prove gold in a box. A classroom does not certify mines.

NOTE
A big holder is not a promise of price, listing, or vaults. Concentration is a fact you may note. It is not a hunting list. Screenshots of holder tabs are as fakeable as any other screenshot — the next lesson is that distrust, made systematic.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Holders are now a statistic with manners. Next: logs, method names, and approve as something you can see — still without teaching Solidity.

## Say this out loud

- The token tracker is identity plus history plus a holder list, not a shop.
- A large balance may be a pool, a CEX, a treasury, or a person. Labels can be wrong.
- A big holder is not a promise of price, listing, or a mineral vault.
- Holder concentration is part of the decentralisation test, not a reason to harass anyone.
- Captions about whales that skip the contract address are theatre.

Next: logs, method names, and “approve” as something you can see.

lessons.title: Logs, method names, and “approve” as something you can see
lessons.content:
# Logs, method names, and “approve” as something you can see

You do not need to decode hex. You do need to notice that BscScan often writes a **method name** in English — transfer, approve, transferFrom, swapExactTokens… — and that **logs** are the contract’s receipts.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to find an **approval** after it happened, know that it loaded a spender’s gun, and refuse a decoder site that wants a wallet connect.

## Method names are labels on the instruction

On a transaction page, BscScan often shows a method: **transfer**, **approve**, **transferFrom**, **multicall**, a swap name, or “Transfer” as a native send. These labels are decoded for humans. They can be missing, or a contract can use a weird name. Still: if you see **approve**, you did not “only connect.” You authorised a spender.

**transfer** on a token contract is the usual “send this ticker to this address.” **transferFrom** is a spender moving tokens you already allowed. If you see transferFrom and you were not the signer but your tokens moved, look backward for an approve (or a permit signature) to that spender.

This course will not teach you to write these functions. Advanced is not hiding in a Basic footnote. Reading the label is enough.

## Logs are receipts the contract emitted

**Logs** (events) are how contracts announce “this happened” in a way explorers index. A Transfer event is why the token-transfer tab exists. An Approval event is why you can see a spender and an amount later.

You can open Logs and feel lost. That is allowed. Use the human tabs first: Token transfers, and the Approval line many explorers surface. If you ever need the raw log, you still do not paste it into a stranger’s decoder that then asks to connect.

## Approve as something you can see tomorrow

Module 4 said approve loads a gun. This lesson says the gun is visible on the book.

After you approve (if you ever do, on purpose):

- the transaction status is success
- method may read approve
- an Approval event names the **spender** and the **amount** (unlimited often shows as a huge integer)
- your token balance may not have changed yet
- later, a transferFrom can empty you without a popup that looks like send

You can also use BscScan’s token-approval checker tools **on the real domain** as a read-only view, when you are ready. Safety will labour revoking. Today: know you can see it. Revoking is a later transaction that costs BNB. A site that revokes by taking a seed is not revoking. It is emptying.

TABLE
What you see | What it usually meant | What to do
Method: transfer | A token send | Check token contract, amount, recipient
Method: approve | Loaded a spender | Name the spender; if unknown, treat as incident
Method: transferFrom | Spender moved tokens | Find the earlier approve/permit
Method: swap… / multicall | A program bundle | Check end balances versus intent
Logs: Approval | Receipt of allowance | Same as approve
Logs: Transfer | Receipt of a token move | Same as token-transfer tab
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Last month a student tapped Approve on a “dashboard.” Today USDT is gone.

1. They open their address on BscScan. They do not download a helper APK.
2. They find a successful **approve** from last month, spender they do not recognise, amount unlimited.
3. They find today’s **transferFrom**, same spender, their USDT leaving.
4. The chain is consistent. The missing skill was reading the popup last month, and reading the method name today.
5. Safety will teach incident response. This lesson only proves the book still shows the gun and the shot. They still do not paste a seed to “reverse logs.”

DIAGRAM
Approve tx
  method: approve
  log: Approval(spender, amount)
        |
        v
Days later
  method: transferFrom
  log: Transfer(you -> attacker)
        |
        v
Balance gone; book still honest; helper who wants a seed is the second shot
ENDDIAGRAM

## You still do not need hex

If method is blank, use token transfers and the to-address. If you see gibberish input data, do not become a hobby decoder this week. Blank plus a mystery **to** plus an approve-shaped token row is enough to stop and not retry.

BscScan sometimes shows **Approve (Spender)** in a friendly box. That box is the lesson. Write the spender address in your notes if you are studying an incident. Compare it to the router you thought you were using — if you were using one on purpose. If you cannot name the spender, you should not have approved it, and you should not approve it now “to see what happens.”

You will not be asked to call Write Contract to mint, pause, or launch anything. Those buttons exist. They are not homework. Curious clicking on Write is how people donate.

NOTE
You do not need Solidity to see an approve. Method names and Approval events are enough. A decoder that asks to connect a wallet is not a classroom tool. Verified bytecode still does not mean a safe investment. This academy will not ask you to approve a spender to “complete the lesson.”
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Approvals are now visible objects, not moods. Last lesson of the module: distrust a screenshot of BscScan, because HTML is cheap and edited pixels are cheaper.

## Say this out loud

- Method names like transfer, approve, and transferFrom are human labels on an instruction. They are not hex homework.
- Logs are receipts. Transfer events feed the token tab. Approval events show a spender and an amount.
- An approve can succeed without moving tokens yet. That is the gun, not the shot.
- transferFrom is often the shot that uses an earlier approve.
- Do not paste input data into a decoder that wants a wallet connect.

Next: how to distrust a screenshot of BscScan.

lessons.title: How to distrust a screenshot of BscScan
lessons.content:
# How to distrust a screenshot of BscScan

HTML is cheap. Image editors are cheaper. A green tick on a PNG is not a page of the book. This lesson is how you refuse payment theatre, fake explorers, and cropped hashes.

By the end you should paste, not squint, and you should treat “check this screenshot” as “give me a hash for my bookmark.”

## Anyone can draw an explorer

A scammer can:

- clone the BscScan layout with one extra letter in the domain
- screenshot a real page and edit the amount
- screenshot a testnet page and crop the word testnet
- screenshot a successful transfer of a **clone token** with the same sticker
- show pending as success with a green overlay
- show someone else’s address as yours

Your defence is not a sharper eye for pixels. Your defence is **independent retrieval**: you open the real domain from a bookmark, you paste the hash or the address, you read the live page.

If they will not give a hash, they have not shown you a page of the book. Module 1 already said this about fake explorers. Now it is a habit with a checklist.

## Domain, network, contract, amount, your address

When someone sends a picture:

1. Ask for the **tx hash** as text, or the address as text. If they refuse, you are done.
2. Open **bscscan.com** from your bookmark — not from their link.
3. Paste. Confirm you are not on testnet unless you meant testnet.
4. Confirm the **token contract** if it is a token payment. Crystal Stones means 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00, not a lookalike.
5. Confirm **your** address as recipient, the amount, and status success — not pending, not fail.
6. Ignore ads. Do not connect. Do not download their “verifier app.”

A screenshot that matches the live page is redundant. A screenshot that disagrees with the live page is a lie. A screenshot with no hash is a poster.

TABLE
They send | You do | You do not
PNG of a green tick | Ask for hash, paste into your bookmark | Ship goods
Link that looks like BscScan | Type bscscan.com yourself, paste the hash | Click through, then connect
Testnet cropped | Check the network chip on the live page | Treat fake coins as local currency
Clone token success | Compare contract character by character | Trust the sticker
“Private explorer” | Refuse | Enter a seed to “decrypt the page”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A buyer sends a crisp screenshot: 1,200 USDT to Amaka, BscScan chrome, green success, her 0x visible.

1. She asks for the hash as text. They stall. They send another screenshot, zoomed.
2. She still does not ship.
3. They send a link. She does not click. She types bscscan.com, pastes her address, opens token transfers, filters USDT on the BSC contract she already uses.
4. There is no 1,200. There is a 1,200 of a clone ticker on a different contract in their PNG, or there is nothing.
5. She keeps the goods. She does not argue about pixels. The live book was the argument.

DIAGRAM
Screenshot  -->  pixels (cheap)
Their link  -->  their window (hostile until proven)
Your bookmark + pasted hash  -->  the book this course means

If they cannot give a hash, they have not paid.
If the live page disagrees, they have not paid.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Edited images and “too busy to paste”

People who actually paid can paste a hash. It is one copy. Stalling is a signal. “The hash is in the screenshot, just zoom” is a signal. “Our accountant is offline, ship now, hash later” is a signal.

You can be polite and still refuse. This is the same shopkeeper rule as confirmations, now with distrust of pictures. Safety will add impersonation and fake support. Today: pictures of explorers are not explorers.

Phone screenshots have extra tells you should not over-trust: status-bar clocks, unread-message badges, a URL bar cropped out. A careful thief crops those. That is why the skill is not “spot the fake PNG.” The skill is independent retrieval. Even a perfect screenshot of a real payment to someone else is not a payment to you. Paste your address. Filter the token. See the row, or do not.

Video “screen recordings” of BscScan are the same family, with motion. A recording of a domain you did not type is theatre with a soundtrack. Ask for the hash. Paste it yourself. If they say the recording is enough because they are in a hurry, they are in a hurry to be paid twice — once in goods, once in the coins they never sent.

## Fake explorers versus fake pictures of the real one

Two different lies. A lookalike domain can show a live-looking page that is not the book. A PNG can show the real layout with a fake amount. Independent retrieval kills both: you typed bscscan.com, you pasted the hash, you read your address. If their link was the only way to “see it,” they needed you off the book.

NOTE
A screenshot of BscScan is not BscScan. Independent retrieval — bookmark, paste, live page — is the skill. Ads, clones, testnet crops, and edited amounts are all cheaper than paying you. This academy will not accept a screenshot as proof of tuition either, when paid tracks exist; the rail will be specified, and the book will still be the referee.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is BscScan until it is boring: dossier, hash, three records, holders without prophecy, approve as a visible object, pictures that do not count. Module 6 is the lab: verify without spending, then a map of where this course sits on the Basic track.

## Say this out loud

- HTML and image editors are cheap. A green tick on a PNG is not a page of the book.
- Ask for a hash as text. Paste it into your bookmarked bscscan.com.
- Compare token contract, amount, your address, and status on the live page.
- A link that looks like BscScan is not a reason to skip typing the domain.
- If they will not give a hash, they have not shown you a payment.

Take the quiz. Module 6: labs you can finish without buying anything.

modules.description: Verify the Crystal Stones contract from more than one source, read public transfers, add BSC and a token without buying, collect common failures, and see where this course sits on the Basic track.

lessons.title: Lab: verify the Crystal Stones contract from more than one source
lessons.content:
# Lab: verify the Crystal Stones contract from more than one source

This lab spends zero BNB. You will not buy. You will not connect a wallet to an ad. You will make three sources agree on one string, or you will refuse the string.

By the end you should treat a single banner as insufficient, and you should know what to do when sources disagree.

## Why more than one source

Scammers clone sites and change one character. Search ads sit above the real site. A screenshot of BscScan is not BscScan. One source is how clones win. Two sources that agree is a start. Three is a habit.

This academy references Crystal Stones as a BEP-20 on BNB Smart Chain at:

**0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**

Treat that as a **classroom pointer to verify**, not as the only source and not as a buy order. If the long-standing project site and the explorer disagree, you do not “pick the one with the nicer logo.” You stop.

## Steps — do them in order

1. Write the string above in your notes, by pasting, not by memory.
2. Open the project’s **long-standing official site** the way you already verified it in earlier courses — typed URL, not a Google ad, not a WhatsApp status. Find the published contract. Copy it.
3. Compare character by character with your notes. Upper and lower case matter for checksum. If they disagree, stop and find why. Do not average them.
4. Open **bscscan.com** from a bookmark. Paste the string. Confirm you are on a token/contract page on the real domain, chain consistent with BSC mainnet, not a connect-wallet clone.
5. Confirm the page’s address matches. Look at the contract tab: is source verified? Remember: verified is hygiene, not a safe-investment stamp.
6. Optional third source: a long-standing official social channel you already trust, not a lookalike with one extra letter. If it disagrees, trust the mismatch. Do not “update” to the new one from a DM.
7. Do **not** connect a wallet. Do **not** add funds. Do **not** follow a banner that says “add to MetaMask” on an ad.

You just practised the only identity skill that matters for a token: **independent retrieval from more than one place.**

TABLE
Lab output | Passes if | Fails if
Official site contract | Exact match, character by character | You used an ad, or you skipped the compare
BscScan page | Real domain + exact address | Connect-wallet clone, extra letter in domain
Notes | You have the string written from a paste | You memorised and “fixed” two characters
Wallet connect | You did not | You signed anything
Buy | You did not | You thought the lab required a purchase
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Google shows two Crystal Stones sites. One is an ad.

1. Yemi ignores the ad. She types the URL she already knows, or she uses a bookmark she made in a calm hour.
2. Site A shows 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. BscScan agrees.
3. Site B, from the ad, shows a contract that differs in two characters. A “verify on BscScan” button on Site B points at a lookalike explorer.
4. She does not add Site B’s token. She does not message Site B’s live chat. She keeps Site A’s string, confirmed on real BscScan.
5. She still has not bought. She has refused a clone. That is a completed lab.

DIAGRAM
Source 1: long-standing official site
Source 2: bscscan.com bookmark
Source 3 (optional): official channel you already trust
        |
        v
All agree on 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00
        |
        v
You have an identity, not a buy order

If they disagree --> stop. Do not average. Do not take the DM.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What disagreement means

If the site and BscScan disagree, possibilities include: you opened a fake site, you opened a fake explorer, the project published sloppily, or a migration story is in play. Basic’s move is **stop**. Not “bridge to the new one.” Not “the DM has the new contract.” Module 3 already called surprise migrations hostile. Intermediate can learn how real migrations are evidenced. You do not have to solve it tonight with rent money.

RWA claims on the site still sit in the legal layer. Matching a contract does not prove a vault. It proves you found the on-chain object the site pointed at — if the site was real.

Print the string, or write it in a paper notebook you already use for wallet habits — not in a cloud doc titled “SEED AND CONTRACTS.” The contract is public. Your seed is not. Do not store them in the same photograph. Do not paste the contract into a random “validator” that then asks for the seed to “complete verification.” Verification is eyes on two pages. It is not a form.

If you finish this lab and a friend asks for “the contract,” you may share the public string. You may also tell them to do this lab themselves. Sharing a string is not a buy order, and it is not tech support for a clone they already imported.

## Ads and “add to wallet” banners on the explorer

The live BscScan page may offer a button that adds the token to MetaMask. Prefer your wallet’s own custom-token screen so you see the string you paste. Explorer ad slots have served malware. A banner that says “verify wallet to confirm contract” is not this lab. This lab is two or three calm pages agreeing.

NOTE
Academy staff will not DM a replacement contract. Google ads are hostile until proven. Verifying 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 from more than one source is literacy. It is not a buy order, not tuition, and not proof of mines.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have a repeatable identity check. Next lab: read a public transfer — BNB and a BEP-20 — and narrate from, to, fee, status like a shopkeeper.

## Say this out loud

- One banner is not enough. Compare the official site and BscScan, character by character.
- The Crystal Stones contract this academy references is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 — verify, do not treat that as a buy.
- If sources disagree, stop. Do not average. Do not take a Friday-night DM.
- This lab spends zero BNB and needs no wallet connect.
- Verified source on BscScan is still not a safe-investment stamp.

Next: lab — read a public transfer (BNB and a BEP-20) and narrate from, to, fee, status.

lessons.title: Lab: read a public transfer and narrate it
lessons.content:
# Lab: read a public transfer and narrate it

You will open a real BNB send and a real BEP-20 send on BscScan and write four facts: **from**, **to**, **fee**, **status**. You will not send. You will not connect. You will narrate like a shopkeeper, not like a fan.

By the end you should be able to say a hash out loud without confusing native value with token value.

## What you need

- A bookmark to bscscan.com
- A notebook or a notes app (not a screenshot gallery as your only record)
- Optional: your own address if you have ever received on BSC — or any public hash from the Crystal Stones token transfers tab. Public is public. You are not spying. You are reading a book.

Do not use a hash a stranger DMs you as the only object, unless you paste it into **your** explorer. The last module already taught screenshot distrust. This lab is the positive version: retrieval and narration.

## Part A — a BNB (native) transfer

1. On BscScan, open any recent successful transaction that sends native BNB from one EOA to another. The token-transfer section may be empty. That is fine.
2. Write: from (0x), to (0x), value in BNB, status, BNB fee, whether it is pending/fail/success.
3. Say out loud: “This is native value. To is the recipient. Token tabs can be empty and the pay still real.”
4. If **to** is a contract, write that down. Native BNB into a contract is not automatically a gift to a person.

You have just read a native send. That is half of Module 1’s envelope, made boring.

## Part B — a BEP-20 transfer

1. Open the Crystal Stones token page: 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on real BscScan. Or open BEP-20 USDT if you prefer a ticker you already know. Either works. This is not a buy.
2. Open **Transfers**. Pick any successful row. Open its hash.
3. Write: status, from, to of the **token transfer** (the recipient of the ticker), amount, token contract, native value (often 0), BNB fee, and whether the transaction **to** is the token contract (normal for a token send).
4. Say out loud: “Native value 0. Token tab shows the movement. I was not looking at a failure. I was looking at the wrong row until I opened token transfers.”
5. Open the recipient address. Confirm the token appears in their BEP-20 list, or that the transfer row exists even if they have not added a display sticker.

TABLE
Narration line | BNB send | BEP-20 send
from | Signer EOA | Signer EOA
to (tx field) | Usually the friend | Usually the token contract
to (token transfer) | n/a | The friend
value | BNB amount | Often 0
fee | BNB | BNB (still)
status | success / fail / pending | same words, check token row too
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student is asked in a group: “Did this hash pay 50 USDT?”

1. They refuse the group’s screenshot as proof.
2. They paste the hash into bookmarked BscScan.
3. Status success. Native value 0. Token transferred: 50 USDT, contract they expected, recipient they expected, fee in BNB written down.
4. They answer with those facts, not with “yes I saw green.”
5. If the token contract were a clone, they would say “success for a different object.” They would not say “USDT arrived.”

DIAGRAM
Bookmark BscScan
  --> paste hash
  --> status
  --> from / to
  --> native value
  --> token transfers (contract, amount, recipient)
  --> BNB fee
  --> write it down
  --> close the tab, keys still yours
ENDDIAGRAM

## Pass / fail for this lab

You pass if you have two short narrations on paper: one native, one token. You fail if you connected a wallet, clicked an ad, or shipped goods against a PNG. You also fail if you still say “value 0 means failed” after Part B.

You do not fail for picking a random public transfer. Public transfers are the point. You do not need to use your own money. You do not need Crystal Stones in your pocket. You need the sentences.

If you cannot find a simple EOA-to-EOA BNB send on the first try, open a busy address — an exchange hot wallet labelled on BscScan is fine — and pick a native transfer from its list. You are reading public data. You are not “hacking Binance.” You are practising the shopkeeper voice on a real page.

For Part B, if Crystal Stones transfers are sparse in the hour you look, use any BEP-20 with a verified tracker on the real domain. The skill is the rows, not the ticker. When you return to Crystal Stones, the rows mean the same thing. Write the contract you actually used so you cannot later pretend a clone was the lab.

A narration that only says “it went through” fails this lab. A narration that names from, to, fee, status, and which tab held the movement passes.

If Part A and Part B are the same hash because you picked a swap, write both narrations from that one hash: native line, then token lines, then fee once. That is legal. It also proves you can see three drawers. Prefer a simple send for Part A if you can find one, so the contrast stays sharp.

NOTE
Ads on the explorer that say “your wallet is at risk, connect” are not the product. Use a blocker if you can. Never connect from a banner. This lab spent zero BNB. Narrate from, to, fee, status. Native and token are different rows.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can read a payment. Next lab: add BSC and a token on a practice wallet without buying, so the window matches the book without a claim site.

## Say this out loud

- I can narrate a BNB send: from, to, value, fee, status.
- I can narrate a BEP-20 send: native value often 0, movement on the token tab, fee still in BNB.
- Success for a clone contract is not the payment I named.
- This lab does not require my own funds or a wallet connect.
- A hash I paste into my bookmark beats a screenshot in a group.

Next: lab — add BSC and a token on a practice wallet without buying.

lessons.title: Lab: add BSC and a token on a practice wallet without buying
lessons.content:
# Lab: add BSC and a token on a practice wallet without buying

You will point a practice wallet at chain ID 56 and import Crystal Stones by contract. You will not buy. You will not approve a spender. You may see a zero balance. Zero is a legitimate result.

By the end you should have a window aimed at the right book, with the right sticker, and no extra signatures.

## What you need, and what you do not

You need an official wallet app from an official store — Trust Wallet or MetaMask as **examples**, not endorsements. You need the wallets-course habits: real app, real backup already done, no photographing of seeds today.

You do **not** need to buy BNB, USDT, or Crystal Stones. If you already have a tiny BNB leftover from the exchanges course, leave it. Do not top up because this lab asked. If you have nothing, the display can still show 0.

Testnet is optional. If you use testnet, remember it is fake coins, not local currency, and not this academy’s Crystal Stones. Prefer mainnet display with zero balances over testnet confusion.

## Steps — network first, then token

1. Confirm you are in the official app. If you are not sure, stop and reinstall from the store you already trust. Do not use an APK from a group.
2. Add or select **BNB Smart Chain**. Chain ID **56**. Known RPC. Explorer https://bscscan.com. Prefer built-in BSC. Refuse a dApp popup from a site you just met.
3. Read the network chip. It must mean BSC before you copy or import anything.
4. Add custom token. Paste:

**0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**

5. Confirm the wallet reads symbol and decimals from the chain. Do not type decimals from a tweet. Checksum warning? Stop, re-copy.
6. Look at the display. Balance may be 0. That is a pass.
7. If a popup says Approve, Claim, or Connect to a dashboard, **reject**. You were importing a sticker.
8. Optional: open BscScan, paste the same contract, confirm the sticker you see matches the tracker. Still no connect.

You may also add BEP-20 USDT the same way if you already know that contract from a source you trust. Still not a buy. Do not search “USDT” and tap the first result.

TABLE
Step | Pass | Fail
Network | Chain ID 56, chip reads BSC | Random “BSC Ultra”, QR from WhatsApp
Token | Paste known Crystal Stones contract | Name search, airdrop, Telegram file
Popups | None, or you rejected approve/claim | You approved a spender
Balance | 0 is allowed | You sent BNB to the contract to “mint”
App | Official store | Helper APK
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A practice phone shows only BNB (or shows nothing). BscScan would show Crystal Stones if this address had any. It does not.

1. The student still imports the contract. Display shows 0 CST.
2. A banner inside a clone of the explorer says “Add to MetaMask — limited airdrop.” They do not use the banner. They used the wallet’s own import.
3. They take no screenshot for a group “proof of holding.” Zero is not shame. This course did not require a bag.
4. They confirm chain ID 56 still selected after a reboot, because dropdowns drift.
5. Lab done. No buy. No approve. Window pointed at the book.

DIAGRAM
Official wallet
  --> add/select BSC, chain ID 56
  --> custom token, paste CST contract
  --> display updates (maybe 0)
  X  buy
  X  approve
  X  claim
  X  send BNB to the contract
ENDDIAGRAM

## If import fails

Wrong network is the first suspect. RPC lying is the second. Typo is the third. Re-copy from notes you made in the previous lab, not from memory. Do not “download a token list pack.” Do not pay a site to add tokens.

If the wallet wants BNB before it will even show a custom token, that is a UI quirk or a fake app. Real custom-token import is a display action. Try the official app’s documented path. Do not send gas to a stranger to unlock import.

After import, open your receive address on BscScan (bookmark, paste). If the book says 0 of that token and the wallet says 0, they agree — lab complete. If the book says you hold it and the wallet says 0, you imported the wrong contract or you are on the wrong network. That mismatch is the whole point of this course. Fix the window. Do not buy to “make it show.” Do not claim an airdrop to “force a balance.”

If you share a screenshot of the wallet with a group to prove you finished the lab, crop the full address if you want privacy, but know that the 0x is already public. Do not share a seed. Do not let a “tutor” remote-control the phone to add the network for you. Pointing the window is the skill. If someone else taps it, you did not take the lab.

## If the icon appears with a surprise balance

A spam token can appear without import. That is not this lab succeeding. That is a poison sticker. Hide it if the UI allows. Do not tap claim. The lab is the Crystal Stones contract you pasted, even if the number is 0, even if a fake “Crystal” sits above it with a cartoon dollar amount.

NOTE
Adding a network and adding a token are window actions. They are not purchases, not approvals, and not a reason to scan a QR. Zero balance is a complete lab. This academy will not tell you to buy Crystal Stones so the icon looks nicer.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

Your window now matches the book on purpose. Next: the failure collection — wrong chain, no BNB for gas, fake token, approval drain teaser — so the whole course fits on one page of scars you do not have to earn.

## Say this out loud

- I can point a practice wallet at BSC, chain ID 56, without a stranger’s QR.
- I can import Crystal Stones by pasting 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00.
- Adding a token is not buying it and not approving a spender.
- A zero balance is a valid lab result.
- Claim and approve popups are not part of import.

Next: common BSC beginner failures, collected.

lessons.title: Common BSC beginner failures, collected
lessons.content:
# Common BSC beginner failures, collected

This lesson is a scar list you do not have to earn. Four failures show up so often they have their own smell: **wrong chain**, **no BNB for gas**, **fake token**, **approval drain**. Each one already had a full lesson. Here they sit in one place so your memory can find them under stress.

By the end you should name the failure in one sentence, name the first honest check, and name the trap that pretends to be a fix.

## Failure 1 — wrong chain

You sent BEP-20 when the venue was on ERC-20, or you watched BscScan for a send that lived on Ethereum, or you picked opBNB / BEP-2 / TRC-20 because the label said BNB or USDT.

**First check:** network chip, withdrawal info icon, explorer of that network. Same 0x is not the same pile.

**Fake fix:** a bridge URL, a recovery admin, a “merge chains” dApp. Real fix: open the book you actually sent on, with that book’s native gas, or contact the venue if you sent to a tagged deposit address. Safety will labour incidents. Today: do not double-send while panicking.

## Failure 2 — no BNB for gas

You hold USDT or Crystal Stones and 0 BNB. The wallet refuses. Or you emptied BNB to zero in the same send that needed a fee.

**First check:** address page BNB balance on BscScan.

**Fake fix:** “send gas to this helper to unlock.” Real gas is taken inside your transaction from your own BNB. Real fix: get a small amount of BNB **on BSC** into **your** address — tiny, from a venue or a person you actually know — not to a contract, not to a stranger’s “unlocker.”

Failed transactions can still burn the BNB you did have. Do not retry a clone five times.

## Failure 3 — fake token

You added by name search, claimed an airdrop, or trusted a screenshot of a clone. The sticker said Crystal Stones. The contract did not.

**First check:** character-by-character compare with 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on real BscScan. Verified source still does not mean safe investment.

**Fake fix:** “migrate to the new contract tonight,” “swap the fake into the real on this DEX.” Real fix: stop interacting. Do not sell into a honeypot hoping to “get some value back” unless you know what you are doing — and Basic’s answer is you do not, yet. Leave it. Learn the paste habit.

## Failure 4 — approval drain teaser

You connected, then approved unlimited USDT to a dashboard. Days later transferFrom emptied the account. Or you are one popup away from that story.

**First check:** BscScan method names and Approval events. The gun is visible.

**Fake fix:** a revoke site that wants a seed, a “support” screen-share, a booster APK. Real fix: if nothing is approved yet, reject. If something is approved, Safety’s revoke-on-the-real-explorer path, with BNB for gas, on the real domain — not a chat link. This course only teasers that path on purpose. Do not improvise with a helper.

TABLE
Failure | One-sentence name | First honest check | Do not
Wrong chain | Same letters, different book | Chip + explorer of that network | Chat-group bridge
No BNB for gas | Tokens visible, door locked | Address page native balance | Mail BNB to a stranger
Fake token | Sticker is not identity | Paste known contract | Name search, migration DM
Approval drain | You loaded a spender’s gun | Method approve / Approval event | Seed-to-revoke, unlimited “just in case”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Four friends in one week, four failures.

1. Sam's USDT is on Ethereum; she is watching BscScan. She opens Etherscan instead of a recovery bot.
2. Bola’s CST display is fat; BNB is 0. He does not pay an unlocker. He notices the fuel gauge.
3. Chika imported “Crystal Stones 2.0.” She compares contracts, stops, does not swap the clone.
4. Dapo approved a dashboard. He sees the Approval event. He waits for Safety instead of pasting a seed into a revoke clone.
5. None of them needed a new religion. They needed the names.

DIAGRAM
Stress
  --> name the failure (chain / gas / fake / approve)
  --> first honest check on bookmarked BscScan
  --> refuse the fake fix (bridge / unlocker / migration / seed-revoke)

The book is still the referee.
Helpers who need keys are not referees.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Honourable mentions, one line each

Pending treated as paid. Failed treated as free. Refresh treated as a chain action. Screenshot treated as BscScan. Sending BNB to a token contract to mint. Testnet coins sold as local currency. RPC that wants a seed. Adding a token believed to be a purchase. Verified contract believed to be a safe investment. Those are this course, compressed. If you can name them, you are ready for Safety’s people-and-programs version.

NOTE
Practice with amounts you can lose. Prefer a test send first when you ever send at all. Academy staff never ask for seed phrase, private key, 2FA codes, or remote screen control. A helper who needs any of those to fix a BSC failure is the failure.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The scar list is now a checklist. Last lesson: where this course sits on the Basic track — behind you, here, and Safety next, with Intermediate still not a licence to launch tokens.

## Say this out loud

- Wrong chain: same 0x, different book. Open the explorer for the network you actually used.
- No BNB for gas: you can see tokens and cannot move them. Do not mail fuel to a stranger.
- Fake token: paste the known contract. Name search and migration DMs are hostile.
- Approval drain: approve loaded a gun you can see later on BscScan. A seed-revoke site is the second shot.
- Failed txs can still cost BNB. Refresh is not a chain action. Screenshots are not the book.

Next: how this course sits on the Basic track.

lessons.title: How this course sits on the Basic track
lessons.content:
# How this course sits on the Basic track

You now have a map of **one** book: BNB Smart Chain. Fluency on BscScan is not employment, not a signal group, and not a requirement to buy Crystal Stones. It is literacy so the next course — Safety — has nouns to work with.

By the end of this lesson you should know what sits behind you, what this course actually certified, what you still should not do, and why Intermediate is not a weekend of launching tokens.

## Behind you

- **Crypto Foundations** — ledgers, keys as power of attorney, the decentralisation test, Crystal Stones as a BEP-20 to verify not to buy.
- **Wallets, Keys & Self-Custody** — who holds the key, seed as backup, send and receive without mixing networks.
- **Exchanges & Your First Buy** — the local currency door, IOUs, BEP-20 withdrawals, tiny tests.

Those three make this course’s examples make sense. If a word still feels foggy — ledger, IOU, seed, withdrawal network — return there. Skipping is how people arrive on BscScan and still paste a seed into an unstucker.

## This course

You can now, without slogans:

- describe a blockchain as sealed pages with hashes
- say BSC is not Bitcoin: chain ID 56, BNB gas, smaller validator set, EVM-like tools
- treat RPC as a window, testnet as fake, BEP-20 as the token rule-set
- refuse the 0x trap and leftover names (BEP-2, opBNB, ERC-20 USDT)
- verify 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 from more than one source
- import a token by contract without buying it
- name gas, nonce, connect, sign, approve, speed-up, cancel, refresh
- refuse bridges for Basic
- read BscScan until the tabs are boring, including an approve you can see
- distrust a screenshot

That is a lot. It is still not “I understand DeFi.” It is not “I should deploy a BEP-20.” It is not “the mineral vault is proven.”

## Ahead

**Crypto Safety & Common Scams** is next on Basic. The people and programs that use everything you just learned against you: phishing, approvals, impersonation, fake support, incident response. You now have enough surface — keys, RPCs, explorers, approvals — that adversaries become the lesson.

**Intermediate** will do contracts and DeFi for real: reading more of a contract tab, using a DEX on purpose, thinking about pools and slippage without treating them as a job. It will still not be a command to put rent in a pool.

**Advanced** is where “how to launch a token” would even be allowed to appear, with the risks attached, not as a side hustle in a Basic footnote. This course did not sneak it in.

TABLE
Skill | Good for | Not a license for
Read chain ID 56 | Correct withdrawals | Trusting every BSC token
Read token transfers | Confirming payment | Ignoring honeypots
Know approvals exist | Pausing a popup | Approving unlimited “just in case”
Verified contract | Hygiene | Safe investment, vault proof, buy order
Add token by address | Honest display | Believing you purchased
Refuse bridges | Keeping funds on one book | Calling every other chain fake
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A cousin finishes this course and asks, “so should I buy Crystal Stones and then bridge to the new chain the group mentioned?”

1. You say: this academy will not tell you to buy.
2. You say: the contract to verify is 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on BSC. Verifying is not a buy order.
3. You say: Basic does not use bridges. Surprise multi-chain DMs are hostile.
4. You say: Safety is next because skill without adversaries is incomplete.
5. You say: RWA claims are claims. A classroom is not a vault receipt.

DIAGRAM
Foundations --> Wallets --> Exchanges --> BSC (here) --> Safety
                                              |
                                              v
                                    Intermediate (contracts / DeFi for real)
                                              |
                                              v
                                    Advanced (not “launch a token” as a Basic trick)

Each course makes the next one’s examples make sense.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What you still should not do

- bridge because a caption said so
- deploy a token because a tutorial skipped the risks
- treat BscScan ads as product UI
- send rent money to a clone because you can now read a hash
- treat testnet as local currency
- paste a seed into an RPC, a decoder, or an unstucker
- confuse USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout (later tuition rail) with Crystal Stones token

Practice, if you practise sends at all, with amounts you can lose. Prefer a test send first.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy is still education. Fluency on BscScan is not employment, not a signal group, and not a requirement to buy the token. Staff will never ask for a seed, a private key, 2FA, or remote control. Paid-track checkout, when it exists, is USDT on BEP-20 — not Crystal Stones, not a DM address.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

The Basic track still has Safety. You have the book. Next you meet the people who lie about the book. Take the quiz. Then go to Safety with your explorer bookmark already made.

## Say this out loud

- I can describe BNB Smart Chain without slogans: chain ID 56, BNB for gas, BEP-20 tokens, BscScan as a window.
- I can verify the Crystal Stones contract from more than one source and still not treat that as a buy order.
- I can match common failures to honest checks: wrong chain, no gas, fake token, approval drain.
- Safety is next because skill without adversaries is incomplete.
- Intermediate will do contracts and DeFi for real. This course did not teach Solidity or how to launch a token.

Take the quiz.

quiz.option_c: Unlimited USDT approve
quiz.option_d: A testnet faucet cashed out to local currency

quiz.option_c: Stop — do not use either until you know why they disagree; do not treat a banner as enough
